## Definition

For degree two, the cell polynomial is $c_{i,0}(1-t)^2+\iota\binom21\,c_{i,1}t(1-t)+c_{i,2}t^2$; this is the displayed Bernstein sum specialized to $n_i=2$.

Let $s\ge1$ be an integer and let $a=x_0<\cdots<x_s=b$ be a finite partition, and on each cell $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ choose an integer degree $n_i\ge0$ and real controls $c_{i,0},\ldots,c_{i,n_i}$. For $t=(x-x_i)/(x_{i+1}-x_i)\in[0,1]$, define the Bernstein basis polynomial
$$B_{k,n_i}(t)=\iota\binom{n_i}{k}t^k(1-t)^{n_i-k},\qquad 0\le k\le n_i,$$
where $\binom{n_i}{k}$ is the natural binomial coefficient from [[def-binomial-coefficient]], $\iota$ is the canonical embedding of [[def-canonical-natural]] into $\mathbb R$, and finite sums use [[def-finite-sum]]. The cell polynomial is $p_i(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n_i}c_{i,k}B_{k,n_i}(t)$. These cell polynomials form a piecewise Bernstein representation. To require continuity at a shared node, impose the additional endpoint-control condition $c_{i,n_i}=c_{i+1,0}$; continuity is not part of the representation unless that condition is imposed.

## Definition

Let $J\ge1$, $N=2^J$, and $x\in\mathbb R^N$, with the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Put $a^{(0)}=x$. For $r=1,\ldots,J$ and $0\le k<2^{J-r}$ define
$$a^{(r)}_k=\frac{a^{(r-1)}_{2k}+a^{(r-1)}_{2k+1}}{\sqrt2},\qquad d^{(r)}_k=\frac{a^{(r-1)}_{2k}-a^{(r-1)}_{2k+1}}{\sqrt2}.$$
The finite periodic Haar transform $T_Hx$ is the length-$N$ vector obtained by listing $a^{(J)}_0$, then $d^{(J)}_0$, then the entries of $d^{(J-1)}$, and continuing through $d^{(1)}$. The input is already of even dyadic length; this convention uses no padding and no endpoint extension.

## Definition

For $P=1$ set $W_1(u)=\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}(u)$, including both endpoints. For an
integer $P\ge2$, define the causal order-$P$ window by
$$W_P(u)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac1{(P-1)!}\sum_{j=0}^{P}(-1)^j\binom Pj(u-j)_+^{P-1},&0\le u\le P,\\0,&u<0\text{ or }u>P.\end{cases}$$
Here $s_+=\max(s,0)$, $m!$ is the factorial of the nonnegative integer $m$
with $0!=1$, and for integers $0\le j\le P$,
$\binom Pj=P!/(j!(P-j)!)$. Convolution means the integral operation
$$(f*g)(u)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(u-s)g(s)\,ds,$$
when the integrand is measurable and integrable, as in
[[def-convolution-of-two-functions-on-rn]]. The displayed formula is finite at
every $u$ and directly defines $W_P$ to vanish outside $[0,P]$; the local
alias lemma proves that it agrees with the $P$-fold convolution of $W_1$ and
establishes the resulting integral, positivity, partition, Fourier-transform,
and derivative identities.

## Definition

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $n,m,p\ge1$, $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, and $C\in F^{p\times n}$. A matrix is **Hurwitz** when every complex eigenvalue has strictly negative real part, as in [[def-hurwitz-matrix-and-continuous-lyapunov-equation]]. It is **Schur stable** when every complex eigenvalue has modulus strictly less than one.

The pair $(A,B)$ is **continuously stabilizable** if some $K\in F^{m\times n}$ makes $A-BK$ Hurwitz. The pair $(A,C)$ is **continuously detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Hurwitz.

The pair $(A,B)$ is **discretely stabilizable** if some $K\in F^{m\times n}$ makes $A-BK$ Schur stable. The pair $(A,C)$ is **discretely detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Schur stable. These are exact existential properties of the given finite matrices. A residual size or an approximate spectral estimate does not itself establish any of them.

A matrix is **Hurwitz** when every complex eigenvalue has strictly negative real part, as in [[def-hurwitz-matrix-and-continuous-lyapunov-equation]]. It is **Schur stable** when every complex eigenvalue has modulus strictly less than one.

The pair $(A,B)$ is **continuously stabilizable** if some $K\in F^{m\times n}$ makes $A-BK$ Hurwitz. The pair $(A,C)$ is **continuously detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Hurwitz.

The pair $(A,B)$ is **discretely stabilizable** if some $K\in F^{m\times n}$ makes $A-BK$ Schur stable. The pair $(A,C)$ is **discretely detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Schur stable. These are exact existential properties of the given finite matrices. A residual size or an approximate spectral estimate does not itself establish any of them.

## Statement

For each integer $M\ge1$, put $H_M=\sum_{k=1}^M1/k$. Euler's constant
$\gamma$ satisfies
$$0\le H_M-\log M-\gamma\le\frac1M.$$
Thus $[H_M-\log M-1/M,\ H_M-\log M]$ is a finite enclosure for $\gamma$.

1.1 For each $n\ge M$, [F1] and [F2] give $$\gamma_n-\gamma_{n+1} =\int_n^{n+1}\frac{dt}{t}-\frac1{n+1} =\int_n^{n+1}\left(\frac1t-\frac1{n+1}\right)dt.$$ The integrand is nonnegative and at most $1/n-1/(n+1)$ on this interval. Therefore $$0\le\gamma_n-\gamma_{n+1}\le\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}.$$ [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Summing step 1.1 for $n=M,\ldots,K$ telescopes to $$0\le\gamma_M-\gamma_{K+1}\le\frac1M-\frac1{K+1}.$$ Let $K\to\infty$ and use $\gamma_{K+1}\to\gamma$ from [F1]. Since $\gamma_M=H_M-\log M$, the claimed two-sided bound follows. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $T>0$, let $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let
$u_0\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$. A measurable
function $u\colon\mathbb R\times(0,T)\to\mathbb R$ is a **locally bounded
distributional weak solution** of $u_t+f(u)_x=0$ with initial datum $u_0$ if
for every bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ and every $T'<T$ it is
essentially bounded on $I\times(0,T')$, and, for every
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$,
$$ \int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(u\varphi_t+f(u)\varphi_x\bigr)\,dx\,dt +\int_{\mathbb R}u_0(x)\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0. $$
The integrals are local: if a test is supported in $I\times[-S,T']$ with $I$
bounded and $T'<T$, the local essential bound makes $u$ bounded on
$I\times(0,T']$, and continuity of $f$ makes $f(u)$ bounded on that bounded
range. The initial integral is finite because $u_0$ is locally integrable and
$\varphi(\cdot,0)$ is compactly supported. This is the local
integrability version of the weak identity in
[[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]], whose
published formulation assumes a global $L^\infty$ bound. This definition adds
no entropy inequality or strong local $L^1$ trace requirement.

## Definition

Let $u$ be an almost-everywhere equivalence class of measurable functions on
$\mathbb R$ with $u\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$,
using the quotient convention of
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], the essentially bounded
class of [[def-l-infinity-on-a-measure-space]], and the local integrability
convention of [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]. For $h>0$ define
$$D_hu(x):=u(x+h)-u(x),\qquad \operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{tr}}(u):=\sup_{h>0}\frac1h\int_{\mathbb R}|D_hu(x)|\,dx,$$
where the integral may be $+\infty$. The **bounded BV class on the line**
$\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ consists of those classes for which
$\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{tr}}(u)<\infty$; we write
$\operatorname{TV}(u):=\operatorname{TV}_{\mathrm{tr}}(u)$.

This translation-variation convention is the standard one-dimensional BV
seminorm on bounded locally integrable classes. It is unchanged by modifying
$u$ on a null set, because each translate of a null set is null. It does not
require $u\in L^1(\mathbb R)$: every bounded constant function belongs to
$\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ and has variation $0$.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For bounded open $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $v\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, put $\varepsilon(v)=(\nabla v+\nabla v^T)/2$. Then
$$2\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2^2=\|\nabla v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2,$$
so $\|\nabla v\|_2\le\sqrt2\|\varepsilon(v)\|_2$.
1.1 For $v\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R^d)$, expanding the symmetric gradient gives $2|\varepsilon(v)|^2=|\nabla v|^2+\sum_{i,j}\partial_jv_i\partial_iv_j$ pointwise. [given, algebra]

2.1 For each $i,j$, apply [F3] to $h=v_i\partial_i v_j$, which is compactly supported and smooth. The product rule gives $\int_D\partial_jv_i\partial_iv_j=-\int_Dv_i\partial_j\partial_iv_j$. Summing in $j$ and using equality of mixed derivatives gives $-\sum_i\int_Dv_i\partial_i(\operatorname{div}v)$. Apply [F3] again to $h=v_i\operatorname{div}v$ and sum in $i$ to obtain $\sum_i\int_D(\partial_iv_i)\operatorname{div}v=\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2$. [F3, algebra, step 1.1]

3.1 By [A1, F1], approximate any $v\in H^1_0$ by such smooth fields in $H^1$. All three squared norms in the identity converge by [F2] and continuity of the finite sums, so the identity passes to the limit. Its nonnegative divergence term gives the displayed inequality. [A1, F1, F2, algebra, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set, and let $1<p<\infty$ satisfy $p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. Then $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is continuously and compactly embedded in $L^2(\Omega)$. In particular, the inclusion is dense. No boundary regularity is required.

1.1 If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)=L^2(\Omega)=\{0\}$ and the conclusion holds. Assume $\Omega\ne\varnothing$. First consider $d=1$. Choose a bounded open interval $I=(a,b)$ with $\overline\Omega\subset I$ and let $L=b-a$. By [F4] and the closure definition [F8], each $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ has zero extension $E_0v|_I\in W_0^{1,p}(I)$: choose $\varphi_m\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ converging to $v$ in $W^{1,p}$ and extend each by zero into $C_c^\infty(I)$. Countable Choice selects this approximating sequence. For every such smooth extension $\varphi_m$, [F6] gives $|\varphi_m(x)-\varphi_m(y)|\le |x-y|^{1-1/p}\|\varphi_m'\|_{L^p(I)}$ and $\|\varphi_m\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}\le L^{1-1/p}\|\varphi_m'\|_{L^p(I)}$, because it vanishes near both endpoints. Applying the second inequality to differences shows that $(\varphi_m)$ is uniformly Cauchy; its continuous uniform limit $w$ represents $E_0v|_I$ since $\varphi_m\to E_0v$ in $L^p(I)$. For every $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(I)$, uniform convergence and $\varphi_m'\to E_0(v')$ in $L^p(I)$ give $\int_Iw\zeta'=-\int_IE_0(v')\zeta$. Thus $w'=E_0(v')$ weakly and [F4] gives $\|w'\|_{L^p(I)}=\|v'\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$. Passing to the limit in the two displayed inequalities gives the same Hölder and supremum bounds for $w$. [A1, F4, F6, F8, given, construct]

1.2 Now let $d\ge2$. Put $s_0=\max(1,2d/(d+2))$ and $s_1=\min(p,d)$. The strict hypothesis gives $s_0<s_1$; set $r=(s_0+s_1)/2$. Then $1<r<p$, $r<d$, and $2<r^*=dr/(d-r)$. By finite-measure Hölder [F3], $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow W_0^{1,r}(\Omega)$ continuously: the function and gradient $L^r$ norms are bounded by their $L^p$ norms, and a $C_c^\infty$ approximating sequence in $W^{1,p}$ also converges in $W^{1,r}$. Therefore [F1] gives compactness of $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)\to L^2(\Omega)$. [A1, F1, F3, F8, given, algebra]

2.1 For a bounded sequence $(v_j)$ in $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$, the representatives $w_j$ from step 1.1 are uniformly bounded by $L^{1-1/p}\sup_j\|
abla v_j\|_p$ and share the modulus $|w_j(x)-w_j(y)|\le |x-y|^{1-1/p}\sup_j\|
abla v_j\|_p$. Arzelà–Ascoli [F7] gives a uniformly convergent subsequence on the fixed compact interval $[a,b]$. Its restrictions converge in $L^2(\Omega)$ by [F5], proving compactness. For each $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ the same supremum estimate gives $\|v\|_2\le |\Omega|^{1/2}L^{1-1/p}\|
abla v\|_p\le L^{3/2-1/p}\|
abla v\|_p$, proving continuity. [A1, F5, F7, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 In the $d\ge2$ branch, for $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$, [F2] and [F3] yield the continuous estimate $\|v\|_2\le |\Omega|^{1/2-1/r^*}\|v\|_{r^*}\le C|\Omega|^{1/2-1/r^*+1/r-1/p}\|\nabla v\|_p$, using the Sobolev inequality [F2] with exponent $r$. Thus the inclusion is continuous on the $W_0^{1,p}$ norm. Finally [F5] and the closure definition [F8] give $C_c^\infty(\Omega)\subset W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ dense in $L^2(\Omega)$. The preceding arguments prove the complete $d=1$ and $d\ge2$ branches; [F9] then gives the claimed compact embedding in its continuous/sequential sense. [F2, F3, F5, F8, F9, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F=\{(x_0,y,z):y_0\le y\le y_1,\ z_0\le z\le z_1\}$ be an oriented rectangle with normal $e_x$, and let $E$ be a $C^1$ vector field near $F$. Orient $\partial F$ by the outward-normal-first convention. Then
$$\int_{\partial F}E\cdot t\,ds=\int_F(\operatorname{curl}E)\cdot e_x\,dS=\int_{y_0}^{y_1}\int_{z_0}^{z_1}(\partial_yE_z-\partial_zE_y)(x_0,y,z)\,dz\,dy.$$
The identities for normals $e_y$ and $e_z$ follow by cyclic permutation of coordinates. Reversing a face orientation reverses both integrals.

1.1 With the stated orientation, the four boundary contributions are $\int_{y_0}^{y_1}E_y(x_0,y,z_0)\,dy$, $\int_{z_0}^{z_1}E_z(x_0,y_1,z)\,dz$, $-\int_{y_0}^{y_1}E_y(x_0,y,z_1)\,dy$, and $-\int_{z_0}^{z_1}E_z(x_0,y_0,z)\,dz$. Apply [F1] to the two differences to rewrite their sum as $-\int_{y_0}^{y_1}\int_{z_0}^{z_1}\partial_zE_y\,dz\,dy+\int_{z_0}^{z_1}\int_{y_0}^{y_1}\partial_yE_z\,dy\,dz$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The two integrands $\partial_yE_z$ and $\partial_zE_y$ are continuous on the compact rectangle, so each is Riemann integrable by [F2]. Riemann–Fubini [F3] identifies each double integral with either order of its iterated integral. Thus the $\partial_yE_z$ term in step 1.1 can be written in the same $dy$-then-$dz$ order as the other term. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Combining the two terms from step 1.1 using the ordering justified in step 2.1 gives $\int_{y_0}^{y_1}\int_{z_0}^{z_1}(\partial_yE_z-\partial_zE_y)\,dz\,dy$, exactly the $x$-component of the curl flux. Cyclic relabeling gives the other coordinate faces; reversing the orientation changes the sign of every boundary and flux term. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $X:=C([0,1],\mathbb R)$ be the real continuous functions on $[0,1]$
([[def-continuous-real-functions-on-a-compact-metric-space]]) with the supremum
norm $\|u\|_\infty:=\sup_{0\le x\le1}|u(x)|$; this is a Banach space by
[[thm-c-k-complete-in-the-sup-metric]]. Fix a continuous real kernel
$k:[0,1]^2\to\mathbb R$. The integral $\int_0^1$ below is the ordinary Riemann
integral, equivalently the Riemann–Stieltjes integral with integrator $y\mapsto y$
([[def-riemann-stieltjes-sum-and-integral]]). For $u\in X$, define
$$(Ku)(x):=\int_0^1 k(x,y)u(y)\,dy,\qquad 0\le x\le1.$$
The integrand is continuous in $y$, so this integral exists by
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]].

A finite quadrature rule on $[0,1]$ consists of an integer $m\ge1$, nodes
$y_1,\ldots,y_m\in[0,1]$, and real weights $w_1,\ldots,w_m$. It acts on a
function $g$ defined at the nodes by
$$Q(g):=\sum_{j=1}^m w_jg(y_j).$$
Its Nyström operator is the finite-sum rule
$$(K_Q u)(x):=Q\bigl(k(x,\cdot)u(\cdot)\bigr)        =\sum_{j=1}^m w_jk(x,y_j)u(y_j).$$
In particular, for the composite midpoint rule with $N\ge1$ panels,
$h:=1/N$, $y_j:=(j+\tfrac12)h$ for $0\le j<N$, and $w_j=h$, the operator
is denoted $K_N$. The nodes and weights are those of
[[alg-composite-midpoint-rule]].

For a right-hand side $f\in X$, the Nyström equation is
$$u_Q-K_Qu_Q=f.$$
This definition asserts neither consistency nor convergence of $K_Q$ to $K$.

## Statement

Let $X:=C([0,1],\mathbb R)$ ([[def-continuous-real-functions-on-a-compact-metric-space]]),
let $m\ge1$, let $y_1,\ldots,y_m\in[0,1]$, and let
$\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_m\in X$. Define the finite-rank linear map
$$ (Fu)(x):=\sum_{j=1}^m\psi_j(x)u(y_j) $$
and, for $f\in X$, define the square matrix and vector
$$ M_{ij}:=\delta_{ij}-\psi_j(y_i),\qquad b_i:=f(y_i),\qquad 1\le i,j\le m. $$
Then the solutions of $(I-F)u=f$ are in bijection with the solutions $c\in\mathbb R^m$
of $Mc=b$, via
$$u(x)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m\psi_j(x)c_j,\qquad c_i=u(y_i).$$
The nullspaces of $I-F$ and $M$ are linearly isomorphic by
$c\mapsto\sum_j\psi_jc_j$. In particular, $I-F$ is bijective if and only if
$M$ is nonsingular.

1.1 If $u$ solves $(I-F)u=f$, put $c_i:=u(y_i)$. Evaluating $u(x)-\sum_j\psi_j(x)u(y_j)=f(x)$ at $x=y_i$ gives $c_i-\sum_j\psi_j(y_i)c_j=f(y_i)$ for every $i$, which is exactly $Mc=b$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Conversely, if $Mc=b$, define $u(x):=f(x)+\sum_j\psi_j(x)c_j$. By [F1] this lies in $X$. The matrix equation gives $u(y_i)=f(y_i)+\sum_j\psi_j(y_i)c_j=c_i$ for each $i$, so $u=f+Fu$ and it solves $(I-F)u=f$. These constructions are inverse because each reconstructed function has the prescribed grid values. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

3.1 If $Mc=0$ and $c
e0$, set $v(x):=\sum_j\psi_j(x)c_j$. The homogeneous matrix equations imply $v(y_i)=c_i$; hence $v
e0$ and $Fv=v$. Thus a nonzero matrix kernel gives a nonzero kernel of $I-F$. Conversely, if $(I-F)v=0$ and $v
e0$, then $c_i:=v(y_i)$ satisfies $Mc=0$; if $c=0$, the formula $v=Fv=\sum_j\psi_jv(y_j)$ would give $v=0$, a contradiction. Therefore the two kernels are simultaneously trivial. By [F2] this is equivalent to $M$ being nonsingular; [step 2.1] then gives bijective solvability of the reconstructed equation exactly when the matrix is nonsingular. [given, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X\ne\{0\}$ be a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]), let $K:X\to X$
be compact, and let $(K_n)_{n\ge1}$ be bounded linear operators such that
$$\overline{\bigcup_{n\ge1}K_n(B_X)}$$
is compact for the closed unit ball $B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le1\}$ and
$K_nx\to Kx$ in norm for every $x\in X$. Suppose $I-K$ is injective. Then
there are $n_0\ge1$ and $C<\infty$ such that $I-K_n$ is boundedly invertible
for every $n\ge n_0$ and
$$\sup_{n\ge n_0}\|(I-K_n)^{-1}\|\le C.$$
For any $f,f_n\in X$, if $u$ and $u_n$ solve $(I-K)u=f$ and
$(I-K_n)u_n=f_n$, then for $n\ge n_0$,
$$\|u_n-u\|\le C\bigl(\|(K_n-K)u\|+\|f_n-f\|\bigr).$$
The theorem does not assert that $\|K_n-K\|\to0$.
1.1 Since $K$ is compact and $I-K$ is injective, [F1] gives a bounded inverse $(I-K)^{-1}$. [given, F1]

1.2 We claim there are $n_0$ and $c>0$ such that $\|(I-K_n)x\|\ge c\|x\|$ for all $x\in X$ and $n\ge n_0$. Otherwise, for each integer $m\ge1$, failure of the bound $c=1/m$ for all $n\ge m$ gives an index $n_m\ge m$ and a unit vector $x_m$ with $\|(I-K_{n_m})x_m\|<1/m$; [A1] permits choosing such a sequence. Then $x_m=(I-K_{n_m})x_m+K_{n_m}x_m.$ The sequence $(K_{n_m}x_m)$ lies in the compact closure of the union in the Statement, so [F2] gives a convergent subsequence, say $K_{n_{m_j}}x_{m_j}\to y$. The displayed identity and $\|(I-K_{n_{m_j}})x_{m_j}\|\to0$ imply $x_{m_j}\to y$, hence $\|y\|=1$. [given, A1, F2, choose]

2.1 By [F3], choose $M<\infty$ bounding the norms of all vectors in the compact union closure. Every $K_n$ maps the unit ball into this closure, so [F5] gives $\|K_n\|\le M$ for all $n$. Along the subsequence in step 1.2, $\|K_{n_{m_j}}x_{m_j}-K_{n_{m_j}}y\|\le M\|x_{m_j}-y\|\to0,$ while pointwise convergence for the fixed vector $y$ gives $K_{n_{m_j}}y\to Ky$. Therefore the same sequence converges to both $y$ and $Ky$, so $Ky=y$. This contradicts injectivity of $I-K$ because $\|y\|=1$. [given, F3, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The contradiction in step 2.1 establishes the eventual lower bound claimed in step 1.2, so each $I-K_n$ is injective for $n\ge n_0$. Its unit-ball image is contained in the compact closure from the Statement, so $K_n$ is compact by [F4]; applying [F1] to each $K_n$ makes $I-K_n$ surjective with bounded inverse. For $z=(I-K_n)x$, the same lower bound gives $\|(I-K_n)^{-1}z\|=\|x\|\le c^{-1}\|z\|$, hence the inverse norms are uniformly at most $C:=c^{-1}$. [given, F1, F4, step 1.2, step 2.1]
4.1 Subtracting the equations gives $(I-K_n)(u_n-u)=f_n-f+(K_n-K)u.$ Applying the inverse from step 3.1 and the triangle inequality yields the stated error estimate. [given, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and locally Lipschitz map $u:U\to\mathbb R^m$ (each point has a neighborhood on which $|u(y)-u(z)|\le L|y-z|$ for some finite $L$, [[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]), $u$ is Frechet differentiable outside a null subset of $U$. Here Frechet differentiability at $x$ means that a linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ satisfies $u(x+h)=u(x)+Ah+o(|h|)$.

1.1 Fix a scalar component and a ball compactly contained in a neighborhood where it is $L$-Lipschitz. Each coordinate section is Lipschitz, hence absolutely continuous by [F2], and has a derivative almost everywhere by [F3], bounded by $L$. For measurability, write the limsup and liminf of the coordinate difference quotients as countable suprema and infima over rational increments; continuity of the section makes these equal the corresponding real-increment limits. Define $g_i$ by their common finite limit where it exists and by zero elsewhere. Fubini makes the measurable exceptional set have Lebesgue measure zero; [F11] converts it to closed-cube-cover nullity. The continuous function is an ACL representative, so [F1] gives $D_i u=g_i$ weakly and $u\in W^{1,\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F10, F11, given, construct]

2.1 Outside a null set, $x$ is a strong Lebesgue point of $g=(g_1,\ldots,g_n)$. For each rational vector $q\in\mathbb Q^n$, apply [F4] locally to the scalar functions $|g-q|$ and to the components of $g$. On a fixed bounded Lipschitz ball these functions are integrable; extend them by zero to $\mathbb R^n$ to apply [F4], and restrict to interior points, where sufficiently small ball averages are unchanged. For each application, the almost-everywhere conclusion provides a measurable Lebesgue-measure-zero set containing the exceptions. Convert that set to closed-cube-cover nullity by [F11], then remove the countable union of these cube-cover-null sets using [F6]. At each remaining point, for every rational $q$, $$\limsup_{r\downarrow0}\frac{1}{\lambda(B(x,r))}\int_{B(x,r)}|g(y)-g(x)|\,dy\le 2|q-g(x)|.$$ Rational vectors approximate $g(x)$ by [F10], so this limit is zero. The rational balls whose closures lie in neighborhoods on which the chosen component is Lipschitz form a countable cover of $U$: local Lipschitz continuity gives a suitable ball around each point, density of rational centers/radii gives a rational subball, and [A1] selects one Lipschitz neighborhood and constant for each such ball. Apply the local argument on these balls. [A1, F4, F6, F10, F11, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Fix such a point $x$, put $p=g(x)$, and on $B(x,r)\Subset U$ set $w(y)=u(y)-u(x)-p\cdot(y-x)$. The function $w$ is bounded on this ball. By [F1] and linearity of the test-function identity, its weak gradient is $g(y)-p$, which is bounded there; thus $w\in W^{1,1}(B(x,r))$ by [F9]. Also $w(x)=0$ and $w$ is $(L+|p|)$-Lipschitz. The strong Lebesgue-point property and [F8] give $\int_{B(x,r)}|Dw|=o(r^n)$. Applying [F5] yields $$\int_{B(x,r)}|w-w_{B(x,r)}|=o(r^{n+1}).$$ [F1, F5, F8, F9, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Write $M=L+|p|$. If $M=0$, $w$ vanishes on every sufficiently small ball. Otherwise fix $\epsilon>0$. ## Statement

The pair $(h,g)$ in [[def-na-daubechies-d4-filter]] is admissible in [[def-na-periodic-orthogonal-compact-filter-dwt]]. In addition, $\sum_{j=0}^3j^rg_j=0$ for $r=0,1$, so the high-pass filter annihilates constant and affine data.

1.1 Write $r=\sqrt3$. Direct addition gives $\sum h_j=8/(4\sqrt2)=\sqrt2$. The numerator of $\sum g_j$ is $(1-r)-(3-r)+(3+r)-(1+r)=0$, and the numerator of $\sum jg_j$ is $-(3-r)+2(3+r)-3(1+r)=0$. Thus $g$ has the required zero sum and two vanishing moments. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 With denominator $32$, the numerator of $\sum h_j^2$ is $(4+2r)+(12+6r)+(12-6r)+(4-2r)=32$, so the zero-shift autocorrelation is $1$. The only possible nonzero even-shift autocorrelation of a four-tap filter is at shift $2$ or $-2$; at shift $2$ its numerator is $(3-r)(1+r)+(1-r)(3+r)=2r-2r=0$, and the shift $-2$ sum is the same by reindexing. Reversal with alternating signs gives $\sum g_j^2=1$ and $\sum g_jg_{j-2}=h_3h_1+h_2h_0=0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For the cross-correlation $\sum_jh_jg_{j-2s}$, only $s=-1,0,1$ can have overlapping taps. These sums are respectively $h_0g_2+h_1g_3=h_0h_1-h_1h_0=0$, $h_0g_0+h_1g_1+h_2g_2+h_3g_3=0$ by pairwise cancellation, and $h_2g_0+h_3g_1=h_2h_3-h_3h_2=0$. For all other integers $s$ the supports do not overlap, so the sum is zero. Together with steps 1.1 and 1.2 this verifies every condition in [F2]. [step 1.1, step 1.2, given, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $f\in\mathcal S^1$ with $M_1=M_1(f)$. For every integer $J\ge0$, with $h=2^{-J}$ and $P_J$ as in [[def-na-haar-cell-average-projection]],
$$\left(\int_0^1|f(x)-P_Jf(x)|^2\,dx\right)^{1/2}\le \frac{h}{\sqrt2}M_1.$$
Thus the cell-average Haar approximation has first-order error on the explicit derivative-bounded smooth class $\mathcal S^1$.

1.1 Fix one cell $I$ of length $h$ and put $\bar f_I=h^{-1}\int_If$. Expanding both sides gives $\int_I|f(x)-\bar f_I|^2\,dx=\frac1{2h}\int_I\int_I|f(x)-f(y)|^2\,dy\,dx,$ because each side equals $\int_If^2-h^{-1}(\int_If)^2$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For $x,y\in I$, [F3] and [F2] give $|f(x)-f(y)|\le M_1|x-y|\le M_1h$. Hence the double integral in step 1.1 is at most $h^2M_1^2\cdot h^2$, so $\int_I|f-\bar f_I|^2\le h^3M_1^2/2$. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]
3.1 There are $1/h$ cells with disjoint interiors. Summing their squared errors gives $\|f-P_Jf\|_2^2\le h^2M_1^2/2$. Taking nonnegative square roots proves the stated bound. [step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $U\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ satisfy $U^TU=UU^T=I_N$, let $x\in\mathbb R^N$, and set $c=Ux$. For any $S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ let $P_Sc$ retain exactly the coordinates in $S$. Then
$$\|x-U^TP_Sc\|_2^2=\sum_{i\notin S}|c_i|^2.$$
Consequently, for every $0\le m\le N$, $H_m(c)$ from [[def-na-hard-soft-coefficient-thresholding]] minimizes reconstruction error over all choices retaining at most $m$ coefficients. Its squared error is exactly the sum of the discarded squared coefficients.
1.1 Since $U^TU=I_N$, $x=U^Tc$. Orthogonality gives $\|x-U^TP_Sc\|_2^2=\|U^T(c-P_Sc)\|_2^2=\|c-P_Sc\|_2^2=\sum_{i\notin S}|c_i|^2.$ This proves the exact discarded-tail identity. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Minimizing the tail is equivalent to maximizing $\sum_{i\in S}|c_i|^2$ among sets with at most $m$ indices. A maximizing set can include no zero coefficient while omitting a nonzero one; and if it includes $j$ while omitting $i$ with $|c_i|>|c_j|$, replacing $j$ by $i$ strictly increases that sum. Since the index set is finite, a maximizing set exists, and every set of $m$ largest absolute coefficients is maximizing; when fewer than $m$ coefficients are nonzero, adding zero coordinates changes no error. By [F2], $H_m$ is one such set, proving optimality including ties and the endpoints $m=0,N$. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $U\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ satisfy $U^TU=UU^T=I_N$, let $x\in\mathbb R^N$, and set $c=Ux$. For any $S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ let $P_Sc$ retain exactly the coordinates in $S$. Then
$$\|x-U^TP_Sc\|_2^2=\sum_{i\notin S}|c_i|^2.$$
Consequently, for every $0\le m\le N$, $H_m(c)$ from [[def-na-hard-soft-coefficient-thresholding]] minimizes reconstruction error over all choices retaining at most $m$ coefficients. Its squared error is exactly the sum of the discarded squared coefficients.
1.1 Since $U^TU=I_N$, $x=U^Tc$. Orthogonality gives $\|x-U^TP_Sc\|_2^2=\|U^T(c-P_Sc)\|_2^2=\|c-P_Sc\|_2^2=\sum_{i\notin S}|c_i|^2.$ This proves the exact discarded-tail identity. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Minimizing the tail is equivalent to maximizing $\sum_{i\in S}|c_i|^2$ among sets with at most $m$ indices. A maximizing set can include no zero coefficient while omitting a nonzero one; and if it includes $j$ while omitting $i$ with $|c_i|>|c_j|$, replacing $j$ by $i$ strictly increases that sum. Since the index set is finite, a maximizing set exists, and every set of $m$ largest absolute coefficients is maximizing; when fewer than $m$ coefficients are nonzero, adding zero coordinates changes no error. By [F2], $H_m$ is one such set, proving optimality including ties and the endpoints $m=0,N$. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Input: a finite set of exact dyadic points in dimension $d=2$ or $d=3$, with
unique stable integer IDs, an ordered tuple with pairwise distinct IDs of the
required size, the coefficient order of
[[def-complete-ordered-real-field]], and an explicit caller declaration that this algorithm uses
symbolic tie-breaking. If an ID is repeated, return the ordinary exact zero
for the repeated-row determinant. Otherwise order all coordinate slots by
point ID and then coordinate index; let $k$ be the zero-based rank of a slot.
Form the requested orientation or lifted
determinant polynomial after replacing that coordinate $x$ formally by
$x+\varepsilon^{3^k}$. Expand with exact dyadic coefficients, combine equal
powers of the formal positive infinitesimal $\varepsilon$, discard zero
coefficients, and return the sign of the coefficient with the least remaining
exponent.

This is a symbolic procedure: no numeric $\varepsilon$ is chosen or
evaluated. It supplies a tie sign only to algorithms that declare this same
shared point-index perturbation. The ordinary exact predicate continues to
return zero on an exact zero determinant.

source_excerpts.text:
## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and use the full-rank cell and angular frequencies of
[[def-ewald-three-dimensional-periodic-source-data]]. Here $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$
denotes the Schwartz space of smooth functions whose derivatives decay faster
than every inverse polynomial. For $\alpha>0$ let
$$g_\alpha(x)=\frac{\alpha^3}{\pi^{3/2}}e^{-\alpha^2|x|^2}.$$
For every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ the two series below converge absolutely, locally
uniformly in $x$, and
$$\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}g_\alpha(x+\lambda)= \frac1V\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3} e^{-|\kappa_k|^2/(4\alpha^2)}e^{i\kappa_k\cdot x}.$$
The lattice Poisson theorem is applied only to this Schwartz Gaussian; it is not
applied to a compactly supported or finite-smoothness assignment window.

1.1 Put $t=\alpha^2/\pi>0$. By [F2], the Fourier transform of $e^{-\pi t|x|^2}$ is $t^{-3/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}$. Multiplying the input by $\alpha^3/\pi^{3/2}$ cancels $t^{-3/2}=(\pi/\alpha^2)^{3/2}$, so $\widehat g_\alpha(\xi)=e^{-\pi^2|\xi|^2/\alpha^2}.$ Each derivative of $g_\alpha$ is a polynomial times $e^{-\alpha^2|x|^2}$. For every degree $d$ and integer $N$, choose an integer $m>(d+N)/2$; the inequality $e^y\ge y^m/m!$ for $y\ge0$ bounds $|x|^d(1+|x|)^Ne^{-\alpha^2|x|^2}$ on $|x|\ge1$, and continuity bounds it on the unit ball. Hence $g_\alpha\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$, so [F1] applies. [given, A1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F1] to $g_\alpha$. Every $\xi\in\Lambda^*$ has the unique form $\xi=A^{-T}k$ with $k\in\mathbb Z^3$; by [F4], $2\pi\xi=\kappa_k$. Therefore $\pi^2|\xi|^2/\alpha^2=|\kappa_k|^2/(4\alpha^2)$ and $e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot x}=e^{i\kappa_k\cdot x}$. Substitution in the periodization formula gives exactly the displayed reciprocal series, and [F1] supplies absolute convergence on both sides. [A1, F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For an invertible real $3\times3$ matrix $B$, put
$\Gamma=B\mathbb Z^3$ and
$$C_B=\bigl(2\|B^{-1}\|_2(1+\sqrt3\|B\|_2)+1\bigr)^3.$$
Here $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean operator norm. Uniformly over every
translate $y+\Gamma$ and every integer shell $m\ge0$,
$$\#\{z\in y+\Gamma:m\le|z|<m+1\}\le C_B(m+1)^3.$$

For $\beta>0$, any integer $p\ge0$, and integer $M\ge0$, set
$$T_p(\beta,M)=\sum_{m=M}^{\infty}(m+1)^p e^{-\beta m^2}.$$
For any integer $J\ge M$ satisfying $2\beta J(J+1)\ge p$, define
$$I_0(J,\beta)=\frac{\sqrt\pi}{2\sqrt\beta}\operatorname{erfc}(\sqrt\beta J),\quad I_1(J,\beta)=\frac{e^{-\beta J^2}}{2\beta},$$
and recursively for $2\le s\le p$,
$$I_s(J,\beta)=\frac{J^{s-1}e^{-\beta J^2}}{2\beta} +\frac{s-1}{2\beta}I_{s-2}(J,\beta).$$
Then the finite controller
$$U_p(\beta,M,J)=\sum_{m=M}^{J}(m+1)^p e^{-\beta m^2} +\sum_{s=0}^{p}\binom ps I_s(J,\beta)$$
satisfies $T_p(\beta,M)\le U_p(\beta,M,J)$. Such a $J$ exists for every
$\beta>0$, $M\ge0$, and integer $p\ge0$.

1.1 Under Countable Choice [A1], use [F1] to replace $y$ modulo $B\mathbb Z^3$ by a vector $y_0=Bv$ with $v\in[0,1]^3$. Thus $|y_0|\le\sqrt3\|B\|_2$. If $z=y_0+Bn$ lies in the shell $m\le|z|<m+1$, then $|n|\le\|B^{-1}\|_2(m+1+\sqrt3\|B\|_2)$. The number of integer triples with this bound is at most $(2\|B^{-1}\|_2(m+1+\sqrt3\|B\|_2)+1)^3\le C_B(m+1)^3$, proving the uniform shell count. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

1.2 Choose $J\ge M$ with $2\beta J(J+1)\ge p$, which exists by [F3]. For $x\ge J$, the derivative of $f(x)=(x+1)^pe^{-\beta x^2}$ has the sign of $p/(x+1)-2\beta x\le0$, so $f$ is nonincreasing. Therefore $\sum_{m=J+1}^{\infty}f(m)\le\int_J^{\infty}f(x)dx$. Expanding $(x+1)^p$ by the binomial theorem gives $\int_J^{\infty}f(x)dx=\sum_{s=0}^p\binom ps I_s(J,\beta)$. [given, F3, algebra]

2.1 The formulas for $I_0$ and $I_1$ follow by the substitutions $t=\sqrt\beta x$ and $u=\beta x^2$. For $s\ge2$, choose an integer $L>(s+1)/2$; $e^{\beta x^2}\ge(\beta x^2)^L/L!$ shows $x^se^{-\beta x^2}=O(x^{s-2L})$ is integrable at infinity. Apply [F4] on $[J,R]$ and let $R\to\infty$; the same inequality makes the boundary term $R^{s-1}e^{-\beta R^2}$ vanish. This gives $I_s=J^{s-1}e^{-\beta J^2}/(2\beta)+(s-1)I_{s-2}/(2\beta)$. Hence the finite sum through $J$ plus the integral tail in step 1.2 equals $U_p$ and bounds $T_p$. [A1, F2, F4, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Use the data of [[def-finite-weighted-network-diffusion-data]]. Let
$E_+=\{e\in E:c_e>0\}$ and let $G_+=(V,E_+)$; its connected components are
the **positive-conductance components**. For $x\in\mathbb R^I$, let
$\bar x\in\mathbb R^V$ equal $x$ on $I$ and $0$ on $D$. Then

$$x^{\mathsf T}L_Dx=\sum_{e\in E}c_e (\bar x_{\mathrm{head}(e)}-\bar x_{\mathrm{tail}(e)})^2\ge0.$$

Consequently $L_D$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and $x\in\ker L_D$
exactly when $\bar x$ is constant on each positive-conductance component and
that constant is zero on every such component meeting $D$. In the closed
case $D=\varnothing$, every differentiable solution of
$Mu'+L_Cu=f$ satisfies

$$\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu(t)=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}f(t).$$

Thus homogeneous closed diffusion conserves weighted mass
$\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu$, which need not equal the unweighted sum
$\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}u$.

1.1 Reversing an edge orientation replaces its incidence column $b_e$ by $-b_e$, but the contribution $c_eb_eb_e^{\mathsf T}$ to $BCB^{\mathsf T}$ does not change. For the zero extension $\bar x$, [F1] gives $b_e^{\mathsf T}\bar x=\bar x_{\mathrm{head}(e)} -\bar x_{\mathrm{tail}(e)}$. Expanding $\bar x^{\mathsf T}BCB^{\mathsf T}\bar x =\sum_ec_e(b_e^{\mathsf T}\bar x)^2$ proves the displayed energy identity. It is nonnegative term by term, so $L_D$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 If $L_Dx=0$, step 1.1 gives a sum of nonnegative terms equal to $x^{\mathsf T}L_Dx=0$. For every $e\in E_+$ its endpoint difference must therefore be zero. Along every path in $G_+$, $\bar x$ has equal values at successive vertices, hence is constant on each positive-conductance component; it is zero on any such component meeting $D$ because $\bar x=0$ there. Conversely, if these componentwise conditions hold, every edge with $c_e>0$ has zero endpoint difference, while an edge with $c_e=0$ contributes zero regardless of its difference. Thus $BCB^{\mathsf T}\bar x=0$ and $L_Dx=0$. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $D=\varnothing$. From [F1], every column of $B$ sums to zero, so $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}B=0$ and therefore $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}L_C=0$. Multiplying $Mu'+L_Cu=f$ on the left by $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}$ gives $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu'+\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}L_Cu =\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}f$. The second term vanishes, and the first is the derivative of $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu$, proving the balance law and its homogeneous conservation case. [F1, F2, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Use the data of [[def-finite-weighted-network-diffusion-data]]. Let
$E_+=\{e\in E:c_e>0\}$ and let $G_+=(V,E_+)$; its connected components are
the **positive-conductance components**. For $x\in\mathbb R^I$, let
$\bar x\in\mathbb R^V$ equal $x$ on $I$ and $0$ on $D$. Then

$$x^{\mathsf T}L_Dx=\sum_{e\in E}c_e (\bar x_{\mathrm{head}(e)}-\bar x_{\mathrm{tail}(e)})^2\ge0.$$

Consequently $L_D$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and $x\in\ker L_D$
exactly when $\bar x$ is constant on each positive-conductance component and
that constant is zero on every such component meeting $D$. In the closed
case $D=\varnothing$, every differentiable solution of
$Mu'+L_Cu=f$ satisfies

$$\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu(t)=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}f(t).$$

Thus homogeneous closed diffusion conserves weighted mass
$\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu$, which need not equal the unweighted sum
$\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}u$.

1.1 Reversing an edge orientation replaces its incidence column $b_e$ by $-b_e$, but the contribution $c_eb_eb_e^{\mathsf T}$ to $BCB^{\mathsf T}$ does not change. For the zero extension $\bar x$, [F1] gives $b_e^{\mathsf T}\bar x=\bar x_{\mathrm{head}(e)} -\bar x_{\mathrm{tail}(e)}$. Expanding $\bar x^{\mathsf T}BCB^{\mathsf T}\bar x =\sum_ec_e(b_e^{\mathsf T}\bar x)^2$ proves the displayed energy identity. It is nonnegative term by term, so $L_D$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 If $L_Dx=0$, step 1.1 gives a sum of nonnegative terms equal to $x^{\mathsf T}L_Dx=0$. For every $e\in E_+$ its endpoint difference must therefore be zero. Along every path in $G_+$, $\bar x$ has equal values at successive vertices, hence is constant on each positive-conductance component; it is zero on any such component meeting $D$ because $\bar x=0$ there. Conversely, if these componentwise conditions hold, every edge with $c_e>0$ has zero endpoint difference, while an edge with $c_e=0$ contributes zero regardless of its difference. Thus $BCB^{\mathsf T}\bar x=0$ and $L_Dx=0$. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $D=\varnothing$. From [F1], every column of $B$ sums to zero, so $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}B=0$ and therefore $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}L_C=0$. Multiplying $Mu'+L_Cu=f$ on the left by $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}$ gives $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu'+\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}L_Cu =\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}f$. The second term vanishes, and the first is the derivative of $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}Mu$, proving the balance law and its homogeneous conservation case. [F1, F2, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Use [[def-na-periodic-staggered-grid-stokes-operators]] with $h=1/N$. For a
smooth periodic vector field $u\in C^4(\mathbb T^d;\mathbb R^d)$, define
$R_hu$ by sampling component $i$ at each face centre $x_j+he_i/2$. For a
smooth periodic scalar $p\in C^3(\mathbb T^d)$, define $R_hp$ by sampling at
cell centres $x_j$. Then uniformly for $N\ge2$,
$$ \|D_hR_hu-R_h(\nabla\cdot u)\|_{Q_h} +\|A_hR_hu-R_h(-\Delta u)\|_{M_h} +\|G_hR_hp-R_h(\nabla p)\|_{M_h} \le C h^2, $$
where $C$ depends only on $d$ and the suprema of the displayed fields'
derivatives through orders $4$ for $u$ and $3$ for $p$. Here the sampling of a
vector field is facewise componentwise. For any $g\in C^2(\mathbb T^d)$ with
zero integral, the cell-centred or face-centred midpoint samples have discrete
mean of absolute value at most $C_dh^2\|D^2g\|_\infty$.

1.1 For $g\in C^3(\mathbb T^d)$, Taylor's formula with Lagrange remainder at the midpoint and [F3] with $m=2$ give $$ g(x+h e_i/2)-g(x-h e_i/2)=h\,\partial_i g(x)+r, \qquad |r|\le h^3\|\partial_i^3g\|_\infty/24. $$ The same midpoint formula, with the two cell centres surrounding face $x_j+he_i/2$, gives $$ (G_hR_hp)_{i,j}=\partial_i p(x_j+he_i/2)+O(h^2), $$ with the pointwise error bounded by $h^2\|\partial_i^3p\|_\infty/24$. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.2 For $g\in C^4(\mathbb T^d)$, [F3] with $m=3$ at $x$ gives $$ g(x+h e_i)-2g(x)+g(x-h e_i)=h^2\partial_i^2g(x)+r, $$ where the two fourth-order Lagrange remainders have total absolute value at most $h^4\|\partial_i^4g\|_\infty/12$. Apply this in every coordinate to $u_i$ at its face centre. It follows that $(A_hR_hu)_{i,j}=-(\Delta u_i)(x_j+he_i/2)+O(h^2)$, with the error bounded by $h^2\sum_\ell\|\partial_\ell^4u_i\|_\infty/12$. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Applying the midpoint formula to component $u_i$ at cell centre $x_j$ shows, by [F3] with $m=2$, $$ (D_hR_hu)_j=\sum_i\partial_i u_i(x_j)+r_j, \qquad |r_j|\le\frac{h^2}{24}\sum_i\|\partial_i^3u_i\|_\infty. $$ Thus the discrete divergence differs pointwise from the sampled continuous divergence by $O(h^2)$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Each pointwise error bound in steps 1.1–1.2 is uniform. The weighted mass of the grid contains $h^dN^d=1$ total cell volume and there are $d$ velocity components. Therefore the corresponding mass norms are bounded by the same constants (or their finite $d$-component sum) times $h^2$. Combining the divergence, vector Laplacian and pressure gradient bounds proves the first claim. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]

4.1 On each cell centred at $x_j$, fix $x$ and put $z=x-x_j$ and $\psi(t)=g(x_j+tz)$ for $0\le t\le1$. By [F3] with $m=1$ and [F4], $g(x)=g(x_j)+\nabla g(x_j)\cdot z+r_j(x)$ with $|r_j(x)|\le C_d\|D^2g\|_\infty|z|^2$. The linear term integrates to zero on the centred cell, so the difference between $h^dg(x_j)$ and $\int_{C_j}g$ is at most $C_dh^{d+2}\|D^2g\|_\infty$. Summing the $N^d$ cells yields $$ \left|h^d\sum_jg(x_j)-\int_{\mathbb T^d}g(x)\,dx\right| \le C_dh^2\|D^2g\|_\infty. $$ The face centres for any fixed component likewise centre a translated partition into cells of side $h$, so the same estimate holds for their samples. If the integral vanishes, this gives the stated discrete-mean bound. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra] ∎

## Example

This is a self-contained one-dimensional interval specialization of the jump convention in [[def-sipdg-jump-average-convention]]. Let $K^-=(0,1/2)$ and $K^+=(1/2,1)$, take unit coefficient, and set $h_F=1/2$ at the interior point face. Define $v(x)=x$ on $K^-$ and $v(x)=x-1$ on $K^+$. Then $v(0)=v(1)=0$, while the interior jump at $x=1/2$ is $1$ and the average derivative is $1$. The face contributions are $-\{v'\}[v]-\{v'\}[v]+\gamma h_F^{-1}[v]^2$. With penalty parameter $\gamma=1$, the bilinear form has value $a_h(v,v)=1$.

1.1 The derivative is $1$ on both cells, so the broken volume term is $\int_0^{1/2}1\,dx+\int_{1/2}^11\,dx=1$. At the interior point $x=1/2$, [F1] gives $[v]=1/2-(-1/2)=1$ and $\{v'\}=1$, while both boundary traces vanish. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The interior consistency terms contribute $-2\{v'\}[v]=-2$, and the penalty contributes $\gamma h_F^{-1}[v]^2=1\cdot2\cdot1=2$. Adding these to the volume term from step 1.1 gives $a_h(v,v)=1-2+2=1$. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Use $\mathcal H_\ell$ from [[def-spherical-harmonic-partial-wave-conventions]]. For every $\ell\ge0$, $\dim_\mathbb C\mathcal H_\ell=2\ell+1$; the spaces $\mathcal H_\ell$ are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\sigma;\mathbb C)$ and their algebraic sum is dense there. Thus they give a complete orthogonal spherical-harmonic expansion. For any orthonormal basis $Y_{\ell 1},\ldots,Y_{\ell,2\ell+1}$ of $\mathcal H_\ell$, the basis-independent reproducing kernel
$$Z_\ell(\omega,\eta):=\sum_{m=1}^{2\ell+1}Y_{\ell m}(\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\eta)}$$
satisfies $Z_\ell(\omega,\omega)=(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)$. In particular,
$$|g(\omega)|\le\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}}\,\|g\|_{L^2(S^2)}\qquad(g\in\mathcal H_\ell).$$
For fixed $\eta$, rotational invariance makes $Z_\ell(\omega,\eta)$ a degree-$\ell$ zonal polynomial of $\omega\cdot\eta$; normalizing $P_\ell(1)=1$ gives the usual addition identity $Z_\ell(\omega,\eta)=\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}P_\ell(\omega\cdot\eta)$.

1.1 If $P_\ell(x)=r^\ell Y(\omega)$ is homogeneous and harmonic, the polar Laplacian convention in [F1] gives $0=\Delta P_\ell=r^{\ell-2}(\ell(\ell+1)Y+\Delta_{S^2}Y)$. Hence $-\Delta_{S^2}Y=\ell(\ell+1)Y$. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Let $\mathcal P_n$ be the homogeneous complex polynomials of degree $n$ in three variables, with monomial basis of size $\binom{n+2}{2}$. For homogeneous $R_m$ of degree $m$, direct differentiation gives $\Delta(|x|^{2a}R_m)=2a(2m+2a+1)|x|^{2a-2}R_m+|x|^{2a}\Delta R_m$. Given $S\in\mathcal P_{n-2}$, put $J=\lfloor(n-2)/2\rfloor$, $c_j=2(j+1)(2n-2j-1)$, $b_0=1/c_0$, and $b_j=-b_{j-1}/c_j$ for $1\le j\le J$. Then $Q=\sum_{j=0}^Jb_j|x|^{2(j+1)}\Delta^jS\in\mathcal P_n$ satisfies $\Delta Q=S$: the coefficient of $|x|^{2j}\Delta^jS$ is $b_jc_j+b_{j-1}=0$ for $j\ge1$, the $S$ coefficient is $b_0c_0=1$, and $\Delta^{J+1}S=0$. Thus $\Delta:\mathcal P_n\to\mathcal P_{n-2}$ is onto. By [F5], its harmonic kernel has dimension $\binom{n+2}{2}-\binom n2=2n+1$ for $n\ge2$; for $n=0,1$ all homogeneous polynomials are harmonic and have dimensions $1,3$. Restriction to $S^2$ is injective because homogeneity recovers $P(r\omega)=r^nP(\omega)$, so $\dim\mathcal H_n=2n+1$. [F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $P_\ell,Q_m$ be homogeneous harmonic polynomials of degrees $\ell,m$. Apply [F2] on the unit ball to the real and imaginary components of $P_\ell,\overline{Q_m}$. Their volume Laplacians vanish, while homogeneity gives outward normal derivatives $\partial_
u P_\ell=\ell P_\ell$ and $\partial_
u\overline{Q_m}=m\overline{Q_m}$ on $S^2$. Therefore $(\ell-m)\int_{S^2}P_\ell(\omega)\overline{Q_m(\omega)}d\sigma(\omega)=0$. If $\ell
e m$, this proves orthogonality. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For $P\in\mathcal P_n$, define $H=P+\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}a_j|x|^{2j}\Delta^jP$, where $a_0=1$ and $a_{j+1}=-a_j/[2(j+1)(2n-2j-1)]$. The differentiation identity in step 1.2 shows that the coefficients of each $|x|^{2j}\Delta^{j+1}P$ cancel in $\Delta H$, so $H$ is harmonic. Since $P-H$ is divisible by $|x|^2$, restriction to $S^2$ writes $P|_{S^2}$ as an element of $\mathcal H_n$ plus the restriction of a homogeneous degree-$(n-2)$ polynomial. Induction on degree decomposes every polynomial restriction into a finite sum of spherical harmonics. [step 1.2, given, algebra]

2.3 Fix $\ell$ and choose an orthonormal basis of its finite-dimensional space. The sum $Z_\ell$ is independent of this basis because a unitary change of basis preserves the sum of rank-one coordinate kernels. For $R\in SO(3)$ and Borel $E\subseteq S^2$, the polar-surface definition represents $\sigma(E)$ as three times the Lebesgue measure of its unit radial cone $C_E=\{r\omega:0<r\le1,\ \omega\in E\}$. Since $R$ is a homeomorphism, $RE$ is Borel, $RC_E=C_{RE}$, and $|\det R|=1$; [F7] therefore gives $\sigma(RE)=\sigma(E)$. If $P$ is homogeneous and harmonic of degree $\ell$, then $P\circ R^{-1}$ is homogeneous of the same degree and remains harmonic: the chain rule and orthogonality give $\Delta(P\circ R^{-1})(x)=\sum_{i,j}(R^{-1}(R^{-1})^T)_{ij}(\partial_{ij}P)(R^{-1}x)=\Delta P(R^{-1}x)=0$. Thus composition with $R^{-1}$ is unitary on $L^2(S^2,d\sigma)$ and preserves $\mathcal H_\ell$; the rotated basis is again orthonormal, so basis independence gives $Z_\ell(R\omega,R\eta)=Z_\ell(\omega,\eta)$. In particular $Z_\ell(\omega,\omega)$ is constant because rotations act transitively on $S^2$. Integrating the diagonal gives $\int_{S^2}Z_\ell(\omega,\omega)d\sigma=2\ell+1$. Polar coordinates applied to the unit ball and its volume $4\pi/3$ ([[cor-volume-of-a-closed-three-ball]]) give $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$, so the diagonal constant is $(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)$. Cauchy–Schwarz for the finite coefficient vector yields the displayed evaluation bound. [F1, F6, F7, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Let $A$ be the restrictions of real polynomials to $S^2$; constants, sums, and products show that it is a unital real algebra, and coordinate functions separate distinct points. Fix $f\in C(S^2;\mathbb R)$ and $\varepsilon>0$. For each fixed $\eta\in S^2$, form the family of open sets $U_p:=\{\omega:p(\omega)>f(\omega)-\varepsilon/2\}$ for all $p\in A$ with $p(\eta)=f(\eta)$. ## Definition

Use the model and notation of [[def-supg-general-convection-diffusion-reaction-model]]. Define $s_b(K)=h_K/\|b\|_{L^\infty(K)}$ when that norm is positive and $s_b(K)=+\infty$ otherwise; define $s_c(K)=\omega/\|c\|_{L^\infty(K)}^2$ when that norm is positive and $s_c(K)=+\infty$ otherwise. For each cell set
$$\delta_K:=\theta\min\left\{\frac{h_K^2}{\epsilon},s_b(K),s_c(K)\right\},\quad 0<\theta\le\frac14.$$
The minimum is finite and positive because its first entry is finite and positive. This scaling gives $\delta_K\|c\|_{L^\infty(K)}^2\le\omega/4$.

For a trial function $w$ that is the sum of a cellwise smooth function and a member of $V_h$, and $v_h\in V_h$, define the element residual $R_K(w):=-\epsilon\Delta_K w+b\cdot\nabla w+cw$, and
$$a_h(w,v_h):=\epsilon(\nabla w,\nabla v_h)_\Omega+(b\cdot\nabla w+cw,v_h)_\Omega+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\delta_K(R_K(w),b\cdot\nabla v_h)_K,$$
$$F_h(v_h):=(f,v_h)_\Omega+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\delta_K(f,b\cdot\nabla v_h)_K.$$
Here $(g_1,g_2)_D:=\int_Dg_1g_2\,dx$ and $\Delta_K$ is the classical Laplacian restricted to the interior of $K$. For $w_h\in V_h$, $\Delta_Kw_h=0$ because $w_h$ is affine on $K$. No stability claim is part of this definition.

## Statement

Use the fixed dimension $d\ge2$ and the finite shape-regular affine simplicial mesh family from [[def-supg-general-convection-diffusion-reaction-model]] and [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Let $u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$, and on each simplex $K$ let $I_Ku=\sum_{i=0}^d u(a_i)\lambda_i$ be its nodal affine interpolant, where $a_i$ are the vertices and $\lambda_i$ the barycentric coordinates. Set $I_hu|_K=I_Ku$ and $M_2:=|\Omega|^{1/2}\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$, using the Euclidean matrix norm for $D^2u$. There is a constant $C_I$ depending only on $d$ and the shape-regularity bound such that
$$\|u-I_hu\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_Ih^2M_2,\qquad \|\nabla(u-I_hu)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_IhM_2.$$
If $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, then $I_hu=0$ on every boundary facet.

1.1 Fix a cell $K$ and a vertex $a_0$. Taylor's formula along the segment from $a_0$ to $x\in K$ gives $u(x)=p_K(x)+r_K(x)$ with $p_K(x)=u(a_0)+\nabla u(a_0)\cdot(x-a_0)$, $|r_K(x)|\le\frac12h_K^2\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$, and $|\nabla r_K(x)|\le h_K\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 The nodal interpolant reproduces $p_K$, so $u-I_Ku=r_K-\sum_i r_K(a_i)\lambda_i$. On $K$, $0\le\lambda_i\le1$ and $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$. The altitude from any vertex to its opposite facet is at least $\rho_K$, hence $|\nabla\lambda_i|\le\rho_K^{-1}\le\sigma h_K^{-1}$ by [F1]. Substitution of the bounds in step 1.1 gives $|u-I_Ku|\le C(d)h_K^2\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$ and $|\nabla(u-I_Ku)|\le C(d,\sigma)h_K\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Squaring the two pointwise bounds, integrating on each cell, summing over the finite mesh, using $h_K\le h$ and $\sum_K|K|=|\Omega|$, and taking square roots proves both global estimates with $M_2=|\Omega|^{1/2}\|D^2u\|_\infty$. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 On a shared interior facet, the affine traces from its two incident cells agree at all facet vertices, so they agree everywhere on that facet; thus the cell interpolants assemble to a continuous $I_hu$. If $u$ vanishes on a boundary facet, all its vertices there have zero nodal values, so the affine trace also vanishes there. This proves both global conformity and the boundary claim. [F1, given, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded connected polyhedral open set, and let a finite conforming nondegenerate simplicial mesh have connected cell adjacency. Let $V_h$ be continuous vector-valued P1 functions vanishing on the boundary, and let $Q_h$ be continuous scalar P1 functions with zero mean. Let $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$, $
u>0$, $	au_K>0$, and $\gamma\ge0$. For the stationary Stokes specialization of [[def-supg-pspg-grad-div-stokes-forms]], define
$$B_h((u_h,p_h),(v_h,q_h)):=
u(
abla u_h,
abla v_h)_\Omega-(p_h,
abla\cdot v_h)_\Omega+(q_h,
abla\cdot u_h)_\Omega+\gamma(
abla\cdot u_h,
abla\cdot v_h)_\Omega+\sum_K	au_K(
abla q_h,-
u\Delta_Ku_h+
abla p_h)_K.$$
For the residual load, set $F_h(v_h,q_h):=(f,v_h)_\Omega+\sum_K	au_K(
abla q_h,f)_K$. Define
$$\|(v_h,q_h)\|_{h}^2:=
u\|
abla v_h\|_2^2+\gamma\|
abla\cdot v_h\|_2^2+\sum_K	au_K\|
abla q_h\|_{0,K}^2.$$
Then this is a norm, $B_h(z_h,z_h)=\|z_h\|_h^2$, and the discrete problem $B_h(z_h,\cdot)=F_h(\cdot)$ has a unique solution satisfying $\|z_h\|_h\le\|F_h\|_{h,*}$, where $\|F_h\|_{h,*}:=\sup_{y_h
e0}|F_h(y_h)|/\|y_h\|_h$. The estimate controls pressure in the mesh-dependent gradient stabilization norm; it does not assert a mesh-uniform $L^2$ pressure bound or convergence.

1.1 Setting $(v_h,q_h)=(u_h,p_h)$ in the displayed form cancels the mixed terms $-(p_h,
abla\cdot u_h)+(p_h,
abla\cdot u_h)$. By [A1], the PSPG residual term becomes $\sum_K	au_K\|
abla p_h\|_{0,K}^2$. The remaining terms are exactly $
u\|
abla u_h\|_2^2+\gamma\|
abla\cdot u_h\|_2^2$, so $B_h((u_h,p_h),(u_h,p_h))=\|(u_h,p_h)\|_h^2$. [F1, A1, given, algebra]

2.1 If this norm is zero, $\nabla u_h=0$ on each cell; continuity and zero boundary values force $u_h=0$. Also $\nabla p_h=0$ on each cell, so $p_h$ is constant on each cell. Continuity across shared facets and connected cell adjacency force one global constant; its zero mean forces $p_h=0$. Thus the norm vanishes only at zero. [A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $z_h$ is in the kernel of the bilinear map, then step 1.1 gives $\|z_h\|_h^2=B_h(z_h,z_h)=0$, and step 2.1 forces $z_h=0$. Thus the linear map from $V_h\times Q_h$ to its dual is injective and, by equal finite dimensions, bijective; the discrete problem has a unique solution. Testing that solution equation with itself gives $\|z_h\|_h^2=F_h(z_h)\le\|F_h\|_{h,*}\|z_h\|_h$. If $z_h=0$ the estimate is immediate; otherwise division proves $\|z_h\|_h\le\|F_h\|_{h,*}$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $\Gamma$ be a polyhedral boundary as in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]. A **conforming surface triangulation** $\mathcal T_h$ is a finite collection of nondegenerate closed planar triangles covering $\Gamma$, with disjoint relative interiors, such that two distinct triangles meet only in a common full edge, a common vertex, or not at all. For $T\in\mathcal T_h$, write $h_T=\operatorname{diam}(T)$ and let $\rho_T$ be the radius of the largest disk contained in $T$; the family is **shape regular** if $\sup_{h,T}h_T/\rho_T<\infty$, and **quasi-uniform** if $\inf_{h,T}h_T/h>0$ for $h=\max_{T\in\mathcal T_h}h_T$.

The conforming **P0 density space** is $X_h=\{\lambda_h\in L^2(\Gamma):\lambda_h|_T\text{ is constant for every }T\in\mathcal T_h\}$. The continuous inclusion $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Gamma)$ follows because each chart Bessel norm controls its L2 norm and the fixed partition is finite. Hence every $\lambda_h$ defines a bounded functional $v\mapsto\int_\Gamma\lambda_hv$ on $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$; thus $X_h\subset H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$. This inclusion makes the single-layer Galerkin method conforming in its energy space.

## Definition

Use the outgoing time convention $e^{-i\omega t}$. On an artificial boundary with outward unit normal $n$, the first-order local impedance condition is $\partial_nu-iku=0$. For the plane $x=R$ with $n=+e_x$, this is $\partial_xu-iku=0$. It is the exact outgoing relation at normal incidence and an approximation for oblique propagating modes; no exactness or uniform small-reflection claim at grazing incidence is part of this definition.

## Statement

Let $Y=(0,1)^d$, $Q=(0,1)^d$, $g\in L^1(Y)$ be extended $\mathbb Z^d$-periodically, and $\varphi\in C_c^1(Q)$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$,
$$\int_Q\varphi(x)g(x/\epsilon)\,dx\longrightarrow\left(\int_Yg\right)\left(\int_Q\varphi\right).$$
If $g\in L^2(Y)$ and $0<\epsilon\le1$, then $\|g(\cdot/\epsilon)\|_{L^2(Q)}\le C_d\|g\|_{L^2(Y)}$. In particular, for $g\in L^2(Y)$, $g(\cdot/\epsilon)\rightharpoonup\int_Yg$ weakly in $L^2(Q)$.

1.1 Tile $\mathbb R^d$ by cells $C_k^\epsilon=\epsilon(k+Y)$. Only $O_d(\epsilon^{-d})$ cells meet the fixed compact support of $\varphi$. On each such cell choose its lower corner $x_k=\epsilon k$. The mean-value bound gives $|\varphi(x)-\varphi(x_k)|\le\sqrt d\epsilon\|
abla\varphi\|_\infty$. By [F3], $\int_{C_k^\epsilon}|g(x/\epsilon)|dx=\epsilon^d\|g\|_{L^1(Y)}$. Therefore replacing $\varphi$ by $\varphi(x_k)$ on every intersecting cell changes the integral by at most $C\epsilon\|g\|_1\|
abla\varphi\|_\infty$; for sufficiently small $\epsilon$, every such cell is contained in $Q$ because the support is compact in $Q$. Extend $\varphi$ by zero to a compactly supported $C^1$ function on $\mathbb R^d$. For all sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the grid sum has only cells in a fixed bounded box, and $$\left|\epsilon^d\sum_k\varphi(\epsilon k)-\int_{\mathbb R^d}\varphi(x)\,dxight|\le\sum_k\int_{C_k^\epsilon}|\varphi(\epsilon k)-\varphi(x)|\,dx\le C\epsilon\|
abla\varphi\|_\infty,$$ since the total volume of those cells is uniformly bounded. Thus the grid Riemann sums converge. By [F3], the change-of-variables identity first holds for $g^+$ and $g^-$ separately; subtracting their finite integrals gives $\int_{C_k^\epsilon}g(x/\epsilon)\,dx=\epsilon^d\int_Yg$ for signed $g$. The cell-corner sum is therefore $\epsilon^d\sum_k\varphi(\epsilon k)\int_Yg$, which converges to the stated mean times integral. [F3, F4, given, algebra]

1.2 The same tiling bounds the $L^2$ rescaling: each cell has $\int_{C_k^\epsilon}|g(x/\epsilon)|^2dx=\epsilon^d\|g\|_2^2$ by [F3], and at most $C_d\epsilon^{-d}$ cells meet $Q$ when $\epsilon\le1$. Summing gives the asserted uniform bound. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 The averaging result applied to every $C_c^\infty(Q)$ test gives convergence of pairings against that dense class. The uniform $L^2$ bound in step 1.2, together with $|\int_Yg|\le\|g\|_2$, lets one approximate an arbitrary $L^2(Q)$ test by [F2] and pass the pairing limit. This proves weak $L^2$ convergence. [step 1.2, F2, F1, step 1.1, A1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge2$, let $A=\begin{pmatrix}d&r^*\\ \ell&M\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ with $d\ne0$, and let $s\ge1$ be an integer. Let $Z_n=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ e_0&Z_{n-1}\end{pmatrix}$ be the lower shift partitioned after its first row and column. Suppose
$$A-Z_nAZ_n^*=GH^*,\qquad G=\begin{pmatrix}\widehat G\\G_b\end{pmatrix},\quad H=\begin{pmatrix}\widehat H\\H_b\end{pmatrix},$$
where $G,H\in\mathbb C^{n\times s}$, $\widehat G,\widehat H\in\mathbb C^{1\times s}$, and $G_b,H_b\in\mathbb C^{(n-1)\times s}$. Let
$$S:=M-\ell d^{-1}r^*$$
be the scalar-pivot Schur complement. Define
$$p:=e_0+(Z_{n-1}\ell-\ell)/d,\qquad q:=e_0+(Z_{n-1}r-r)/\overline d,\qquad G':=G_b+p\widehat G,\quad H':=H_b+q\widehat H.$$
Then
$$S-Z_{n-1}SZ_{n-1}^*=G'H'^*.$$
Thus the updated displacement rank is at most $s$, although it can decrease. This is an exact identity conditional on the nonzero pivot $d$; it makes no conditioning or growth claim.

1.1 Write $e=e_0\in\mathbb C^{n-1}$ and $Z'=Z_{n-1}$. Direct block multiplication using [F3] gives $$Z_nAZ_n^*= \begin{pmatrix} 0&0\\ 0&(ed+Z'\ell)e^*+(er^*+Z'M)Z'^* \end{pmatrix}.$$ Therefore the first row and column of $A-Z_nAZ_n^*$ are $(d,r^*)$ and $(d,\ell)^T$, while its lower-right block is $$M-Z'MZ'^*-dee^*-Z'\ell e^*-er^*Z'^*.$$ [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 Comparing the four blocks of $GH^*=A-Z_nAZ_n^*$ in step 1.1 gives $\widehat G\widehat H^*=d$, $G_b\widehat H^*=\ell$, $\widehat G H_b^*=r^*$, and $$G_bH_b^*=M-Z'MZ'^*-dee^*-Z'\ell e^*-er^*Z'^*.$$ [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 From the definitions of $G'$ and $H'$, $$G'H'^*=G_bH_b^*+\ell q^*+pr^*+dpq^*.$$ Here $q^*=e^*+(r^*Z'^*-r^*)/d$ and $p=e+(Z'\ell-\ell)/d$. Expand them separately: $$\ell q^*=\ell e^*+(\ell r^*Z'^*-\ell r^*)/d,\quad pr^*=er^*+(Z'\ell r^*-\ell r^*)/d,$$ $$dpq^*=dee^*+er^*Z'^*-er^*+(Z'\ell-\ell)e^* +((Z'\ell-\ell)(r^*Z'^*-r^*))/d.$$ The non-fractional terms combine to $dee^*+Z'\ell e^*+er^*Z'^*$, and the common fractional numerator simplifies by distributivity: $$\ell r^*Z'^*-\ell r^*+Z'\ell r^*-\ell r^*+(Z'\ell-\ell)r^*Z'^*-(Z'\ell-\ell)r^* =-\ell r^*+Z'\ell r^*Z'^*.$$ Thus $$\ell q^*+pr^*+dpq^* =dee^*+Z'\ell e^*+er^*Z'^*-\ell r^*/d+Z'\ell r^*Z'^*/d,$$ as required. Substituting [F2] and step 2.1 now yields $$G'H'^*=M-Z'MZ'^*-\ell r^*/d+Z'\ell r^*Z'^*/d=S-Z'SZ'^*.$$ [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The factors $G',H'$ each have $s$ columns, so their product has rank at most $s$. A strict rank decrease is possible when columns become dependent; no exact rank preservation or numerical growth bound is asserted. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $N\ge1$ and $p\ge1$. Suppose the finite quadtree and recursive interaction decomposition supplied to [[alg-planar-laplace-fmm-fixed-order]] are linear-size level-restricted and have bounded lists in the exact sense of [[def-finite-planar-quadtree-fmm-pair-lists]]: $T,V\le C\,N$, $K:=|\mathcal F|\le C\,T$, and $J:=|\mathcal N|\le C\,N$ for a constant $C$ independent of $N,p$. Counting each complex addition, multiplication, division by a nonzero number, coefficient copy, and cell-pair inspection as one operation, the FMM passes and direct near evaluation use at most
$$C_0\bigl(N(p+1)+(T+K)(p+1)^2+V+J\bigr)$$
operations for an absolute implementation constant $C_0$. Hence their arithmetic and list-processing work is $O(N(p+1)^2)$, and therefore $O(Np^2)$ for $p\ge1$. The input quadtree construction and point-to-cell preprocessing are not included; a highly clustered input must report its actual tree depth, node count, and list/traversal counts before a linear-in-$N$ conclusion is made.

1.1 At each nonempty leaf, P2M accumulates $p+1$ moments per resident source, so the total is at most $N(p+1)$ operations up to a constant. The nonempty cells form a rooted connected subtree, so enumerating them by inspecting four children per nonempty internal cell costs $O(T)$ and yields exactly $T-1$ parent-child edges whose two cells are nonempty. On each such edge, M2M or L2L evaluates triangular sums with $\sum_{n=0}^p(n+1)=(p+1)(p+2)/2$ terms, hence at most $O((p+1)^2)$ operations. Empty-child moments are zero and their edges are skipped. Initializing the local vectors costs $O(T(p+1))$, and both this and the $O(T)$ enumeration cost are absorbed in the displayed bound. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For each of the $K$ far pairs, M2L forms $p+1$ coefficients, each using at most $p+1$ terms, so the total is $O(K(p+1)^2)$. L2P evaluates one degree-$p$ polynomial and its derivative at each of $N$ targets in $O(N(p+1))$ operations. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 The recursive list decomposition uses $V$ cell-pair inspections, and the direct near loop uses $J$ particle-pair evaluations. By [F3] no required pair is counted twice or omitted; the work to dispatch the finite lists is included in these counts. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Adding the counts from steps 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 gives the displayed operation bound after increasing one absolute constant $C_0$. The assumptions $T,V\le CN$, $K\le CT$, and $J\le CN$ then give $O(N(p+1)^2)$; since $p\ge1$, $(p+1)^2\le4p^2$, giving $O(Np^2)$. No bound on the cost of constructing the input quadtree or assigning its points was used. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Inputs are finite CARE or DARE data from [[def-standard-continuous-and-discrete-riccati-equations]], finite Schur or QZ sweep budgets, an adjacent-swap budget $K$, a scalar/evaluator work budget $W$, a positive local separation threshold $\eta$, and the exact arithmetic controller or bounded outward evaluator for [[alg-finite-budget-stable-block-reordering-for-schur-and-qz]]. For CARE form $H=\begin{bmatrix}A&-G\\-Q&-A^*\end{bmatrix}$; for DARE form $N=\begin{bmatrix}A&0\\-Q&I\end{bmatrix}$ and $M=\begin{bmatrix}I&G\\0&A^*\end{bmatrix}$. The procedure never forms $A^{-1}$ and does not require a separately supplied ordered basis.

1. For CARE, run [[alg-finite-budget-francis-schur-reduction]] on $H$. For DARE, run [[alg-finite-budget-qz-iteration-with-deflation-and-residual]] on $(N,M)$. Propagate any budget, range, invariant-pattern, or pencil-regularity failure as an explicit inconclusive status. The returned residuals and factor backward-error certificates are those specified by the corresponding supplier items; they are not interpreted as structure-preserving perturbations.
2. On a successful reduction, invoke [[alg-finite-budget-stable-block-reordering-for-schur-and-qz]] with the CARE strict-left-half-plane selector or DARE strict-unit-disk selector and required selected dimension $n$. Propagate every non-ordered result as its explicit status, including boundary-spectrum, separation-inconclusive, swap-separation-inconclusive, arithmetic-inconclusive, range-failure, swap-budget-exhausted, and work-budget-exhausted. The source algorithm's exact product factors and [F6] certify ordering of the represented computed form and preserve the original unstructured reduction residual. For CARE take the first $n$ columns of the updated Schur factor; for DARE take the first $n$ columns of the updated **right** QZ factor, never the left factor. If the relevant exact factor or residual certificate is unavailable, keep the corresponding diagnostic inconclusive.
3. Write the ordered stable basis as $U=\begin{bmatrix}U_1\\U_2\end{bmatrix}$. Estimate $\|U_1^{-1}\|_2$ using the supplied verified linear-residual certificate; if invertibility or a finite bound cannot be certified, return graph-block-inconclusive.
4. Solve $X_0U_1=U_2$ by a finite verified linear solve; do not form an explicit inverse. Set $\widehat X=(X_0+X_0^*)/2$. Compute and report the actual Riccati residual, Hermitian symmetry defect, the DARE matrix $R+B^*\widehat X B$ when applicable, the graph-block bound, and the actual closed-loop spectral certificate. Any failed positivity or stability check returns candidate-rejected; unavailable certificates return inconclusive. No residual by itself certifies the stabilizing branch or a nearby positive $Q,R$.

This is the finite candidate-extraction stage for the ordered Schur/QZ solvers. Its ordering prerequisite is the finite adjacent-block routine and correctness theorem cited above; a successful order applies to the represented computed form, with the separately stated diagnostics still required for Riccati acceptance.

For CARE form $H=\begin{bmatrix}A&-G\\-Q&-A^*\end{bmatrix}$; for DARE form $N=\begin{bmatrix}A&0\\-Q&I\end{bmatrix}$ and $M=\begin{bmatrix}I&G\\0&A^*\end{bmatrix}$. The procedure never forms $A^{-1}$ and does not require a separately supplied ordered basis.

1. For CARE, run [[alg-finite-budget-francis-schur-reduction]] on $H$. For DARE, run [[alg-finite-budget-qz-iteration-with-deflation-and-residual]] on $(N,M)$. Propagate any budget, range, invariant-pattern, or pencil-regularity failure as an explicit inconclusive status. The returned residuals and factor backward-error certificates are those specified by the corresponding supplier items; they are not interpreted as structure-preserving perturbations.
2. On a successful reduction, invoke [[alg-finite-budget-stable-block-reordering-for-schur-and-qz]] with the CARE strict-left-half-plane selector or DARE strict-unit-disk selector and required selected dimension $n$. Propagate every non-ordered result as its explicit status, including boundary-spectrum, separation-inconclusive, swap-separation-inconclusive, arithmetic-inconclusive, range-failure, swap-budget-exhausted, and work-budget-exhausted. The source algorithm's exact product factors and [F6] certify ordering of the represented computed form and preserve the original unstructured reduction residual. For CARE take the first $n$ columns of the updated Schur factor; for DARE take the first $n$ columns of the updated **right** QZ factor, never the left factor. If the relevant exact factor or residual certificate is unavailable, keep the corresponding diagnostic inconclusive.
3. Write the ordered stable basis as $U=\begin{bmatrix}U_1\\U_2\end{bmatrix}$. Estimate $\|U_1^{-1}\|_2$ using the supplied verified linear-residual certificate; if invertibility or a finite bound cannot be certified, return graph-block-inconclusive.
4. Solve $X_0U_1=U_2$ by a finite verified linear solve; do not form an explicit inverse. Set $\widehat X=(X_0+X_0^*)/2$. Compute and report the actual Riccati residual, Hermitian symmetry defect, the DARE matrix $R+B^*\widehat X B$ when applicable, the graph-block bound, and the actual closed-loop spectral certificate. Any failed positivity or stability check returns candidate-rejected; unavailable certificates return inconclusive. No residual by itself certifies the stabilizing branch or a nearby positive $Q,R$.

This is the finite candidate-extraction stage for the ordered Schur/QZ solvers. Its ordering prerequisite is the finite adjacent-block routine and correctness theorem cited above; a successful order applies to the represented computed form, with the separately stated diagnostics still required for Riccati acceptance.

## Definition

Input $A\in F^{n\times n}$, Hermitian $G_0\succeq0$ and $H_0\succeq0$, a finite iteration budget $N$, and a finite arithmetic/range controller. Set $A_0=A$. For each $j=0,\ldots,N-1$, form
$$W_j=(I+G_jH_j)^{-1},$$
and update
$$A_{j+1}=A_jW_jA_j,\qquad G_{j+1}=G_j+A_jW_jG_jA_j^*,\qquad H_{j+1}=H_j+A_j^*H_jW_jA_j.$$
These formulas use no inverse of $A_j$. The companion recurrence-invariant proof establishes exact-arithmetic invertibility and positive-semidefinite preservation. The finite-arithmetic routine separately reports solve, range, and symmetry status.

In finite arithmetic, attempt each solve by a finite factorization routine. Return range-failure or inverse-inconclusive if the computed solve lacks its declared certificate. Preserve the raw matrices, report $\|G_j-G_j^*\|_F$ and $\|H_j-H_j^*\|_F$, and report the actual DARE residual for $H_j$ whenever its inverse is certified. Symmetrization may be used only to form a candidate and must be followed by fresh residual and positivity checks. No exact positive-semidefinite or structure-preserving backward-error claim is made from a rounded recurrence alone.

source_excerpts.text:
## Example

Take one state and one observation, one update step, $m_0=2$, $F=H=1$,
$y=7$, and factors $L_0=L_Q=0$, $L_R=1$. The initial, process, and
measurement covariances are $P_0=Q=0$ and $R=1$.

1.1 The prediction array is $[FL_0,L_Q]=[0,0]$. Its QR upper factor is zero, so $L^-=0$ and $P^-=0$. The predicted mean is $m^-=1\cdot2=2$. The innovation is $v=7-1\cdot2=5$, and its covariance is $S=H P^-H^T+R=1$. Thus the canonical innovation is positive definite even though $P_0$ and $Q$ are singular. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The measurement prearray is $$ Z=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}. $$ Its exact QR gives $L_{11}=1$, $L_{21}=0$, $L_{22}=0$. The solve gives $z=5$, so $m^+=m^-+L_{21}z=2$, while the represented posterior covariance is $L_{22}L_{22}^T=0$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The canonical covariance update is $P^+=0-0\cdot1^{-1}\cdot0=0$ and the canonical mean update is $2+0\cdot1^{-1}\cdot5=2$. They agree with the factor output in step 2.1. The zero posterior factor is admissible by [F3]; no Cholesky factor of a positive-definite state covariance is required. [F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For $x>0$ and integer $k\ge0$, the moments in
[[def-erfcx-moment-sequence]] are finite and positive. They satisfy

$$2xM_0+2M_1=1, \qquad kM_{k-1}=2xM_k+2M_{k+1}\quad(k\ge1).$$

With $r_k=M_{k+1}/M_k$, it follows that

$$r_k=\frac{k+1}{2(x+r_{k+1})},\qquad 0<r_k<\frac{k+1}{2x},\qquad \operatorname{erfcx}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt\pi(x+r_0)}.$$

1.1 The integrands in [F1] are positive. Near $0$ they are bounded by $t^k$. For $t\ge1$, $e^{-2xt}\le1$; the substitution $s=t^2$ and [F6] bound the tail by $\frac12\int_1^\infty s^{(k-1)/2}e^{-s}ds$, which is finite by the Gamma integral convergence in [F8]. The integrands are continuous on every compact truncation interval, so their proper integrals there exist by [F7]. Thus each $M_k$ is finite; it is strictly positive because its integrand is positive on $[1,2]$. [given, F1, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F5] on $[\varepsilon,R]$ to $w(t)=e^{-t^2-2xt}$ and to $t^kw(t)$. These functions and their derivatives are continuous on the compact interval, so all derivatives required by [F5] are integrable by [F7]; the complex-valued integration-by-parts statement is applied componentwise. The boundary terms tend to $0$ at $R\to\infty$; for $k\ge1$ they also tend to $0$ at $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, while for $k=0$ the lower boundary tends to $1$. For the infinite endpoint, choose an integer $m>k/2$; the exponential series gives $e^{t^2/2}\ge (t^2/2)^m/m!$, so $t^ke^{-t^2-2xt}\le 2^m m!t^{k-2m}e^{-t^2/2}\to0$. Passing to the limits in the integration-by-parts identities gives $2xM_0+2M_1=1$ and, for $k\ge1$, $kM_{k-1}=2xM_k+2M_{k+1}$. [F1, F5, F7, L9, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Divide the recurrence with index $k+1$ by $2M_k>0$. Since $r_k=M_{k+1}/M_k$ and $r_{k+1}=M_{k+2}/M_{k+1}$, this gives $(k+1)/2=xr_k+r_kr_{k+1}$ and hence $r_k=(k+1)/(2(x+r_{k+1}))$. Positivity gives $0<r_k<(k+1)/(2x)$. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The integrand in [F4] is even, so $\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2}du=\sqrt\pi/2$. Subtract the integral identity in [F3] and use the definition in [F2] to get $$\operatorname{erfc}(x)=\frac2{\sqrt\pi}\int_x^\infty e^{-u^2}\,du.$$ The increasing substitution $u=t+x$ from [F6] then gives $$\operatorname{erfcx}(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-t^2-2xt}\,dt=\frac{2M_0}{\sqrt\pi}.$$ The first identity in step 2.1 gives $2M_0(x+r_0)=1$; substitution proves $\operatorname{erfcx}(x)=1/(\sqrt\pi(x+r_0))$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For a conservation system as in
[[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]], constant states
$u_L,u_R\in G$, and a constant speed $s$, define
$u(t,x)=u_L$ for $x<st$ and $u(t,x)=u_R$ for $x>st$, and let
$u_0(x)=u_L$ for $x<0$ and $u_0(x)=u_R$ for $x>0$ (values on the jump lines
are immaterial). Then $u$ is a distributional weak solution with initial datum
$u_0$ in the sense of [[def-hyperbolic-system-and-characteristic-families]]
if and only if
$$f(u_R)-f(u_L)=s(u_R-u_L).$$

1.1 Write $u=u_L+[u]H(x-st)$ and $f(u)=f(u_L)+[f]H(x-st)$, where $H$ is the unit step and $[u]=u_R-u_L$, $[f]=f(u_R)-f(u_L)$. Testing against a smooth compactly supported function and integrating by parts on the two sides of the line $x=st$ gives $\partial_tu=-s[u]\delta_{x=st}$ and $\partial_xf=[f]\delta_{x=st}$. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 For every compact $K\subset\mathbb R$, the functions $u(t,\cdot)$ and $u_0$ agree almost everywhere outside the interval with endpoints $0$ and $st$. Hence $$\|u(t,\cdot)-u_0\|_{L^1(K)}\le |s|t\,\|u_R-u_L\|_2\longrightarrow0$$ as $t\downarrow0$. Thus the required local $L^1$ initial trace holds. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 By step 1.1 the distributional PDE identity holds exactly when $[f]=s[u]$, which is [F1]. Step 1.2 supplies the initial trace in either case, so the definition of weak solution gives both implications. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Example

On two equal periodic interval cells of length $h$, consider degree-zero DG for $u_t+a u_x=0$ with $a>0$ and cell states $u_1,u_2$. Compare the central flux $\widehat f_c(a_0,b_0)=a(a_0+b_0)/2$ with the upwind flux $\widehat f_u(a_0,b_0)=a a_0$.

1.1 For the central flux, both faces of cell 1 see the same pair $(u_1,u_2)$ and hence the same flux; likewise for cell 2. Thus $\dot u_1=\dot u_2=0$ and $E=\frac h2(u_1^2+u_2^2)$ has $\dot E=0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For the upwind flux, the two cell equations are $\dot u_1=-\frac ah(u_1-u_2)$ and $\dot u_2=-\frac ah(u_2-u_1)$. Therefore $\dot E=h(u_1\dot u_1+u_2\dot u_2)=-a(u_1-u_2)^2$. In particular, at $(u_1,u_2)=(1,-1)$ the central rate is zero and the upwind rate is $-4a<0$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$. If $d=1$, let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite oriented interval mesh of $\Omega=(a,b)$, $a<b$, from [[def-pe04-one-dimensional-interval-mesh-and-broken-polynomials]]; if $d\ge2$, let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite matching affine simplicial mesh of $\Omega$. Let $\beta\in\mathbb R^d$ be constant, and let $u_h$ solve [[def-pe04-upwind-dg-transport-discretization]] with inflow data $g$. Assume Countable Choice when $d\ge2$, as required by the affine-simplex Green supplier; no choice assumption is needed for the interval branch. Write $\Gamma_+=\{x\in\partial\Omega:\beta\cdot n>0\}$ and $\Gamma_- =\{x\in\partial\Omega:\beta\cdot n<0\}$. For an interior facet $F=K^-\cap K^+$ choose a unit normal $n_F$ from $K^-$ to $K^+$ and write $[u_h]=u_h^+-u_h^-$. In dimension one, integrals over facets and boundary points mean sums with respect to zero-dimensional surface measure. Then
$$\frac12\frac{d}{dt}\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\|u_h\|_{L^2(K)}^2+\frac12\sum_{F\text{ interior}}\int_F|\beta\cdot n_F|[u_h]^2\,dS+\frac12\int_{\Gamma_+}(\beta\cdot n)u_h^2\,dS+\frac12\int_{\Gamma_-}|\beta\cdot n|(u_h-g)^2\,dS=\frac12\int_{\Gamma_-}|\beta\cdot n|g^2\,dS.$$
In particular, zero inflow data give a nonincreasing semidiscrete $L^2$ norm. This result is semidiscrete and makes no claim about a time integrator.

1.1 In the DG equation on each cell take $v=u_h$. The time term is $\frac12\frac{d}{dt}\|u_h\|_{L^2(K)}^2$. When $d\ge2$, since $\beta$ is constant, $-\int_K\beta u_h\cdot\nabla u_h=-\frac12\int_K\operatorname{div}(\beta u_h^2)=-\frac12\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\int_F(\beta\cdot n_{K,F})u_h^2$ by [F2] and [A1]. When $d=1$ and $K=(x_{j-1},x_j)$, [F3] gives the same endpoint identity $-\int_K\beta u_h\,\partial_xu_h=-\frac12\sum_{e\in\partial K}(\beta n_{K,e})u_h(e)^2$. Sum over cells; [F4] pairs opposite normals on each interior facet for $d\ge2$, and [F5] gives opposite normals at every shared interval endpoint. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, algebra]

2.1 Fix an interior facet oriented from $K^-$ to $K^+$ and put $b=\beta\cdot n_F$. The two face terms from step 1.1 and the two upwind numerical-flux terms combine to $-\frac b2((u^-)^2-(u^+)^2)+b\widehat u(u^--u^+)$. If $b>0$, then $\widehat u=u^-$ and this is $\frac b2(u^+-u^-)^2$; if $b<0$, then $\widehat u=u^+$ and this is $\frac{|b|}{2}(u^+-u^-)^2$. For $b=0$ it vanishes. This scalar calculation also applies to the single endpoint quadrature in dimension one. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 On an outflow boundary face, $b=\beta\cdot n>0$ and $\widehat u=u_h$, so the volume and flux terms combine to $\frac b2u_h^2$. On an inflow face, $b<0$ and $\widehat u=g$, so they combine to $\frac{|b|}{2}u_h^2-|b|gu_h=\frac{|b|}{2}(u_h-g)^2-\frac{|b|}{2}g^2$. Faces with $b=0$ contribute zero. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Substituting the interior contribution from step 2.1 and the boundary contributions from step 2.2 into the sum of the tested DG equations gives the displayed identity. All terms on the left after the time derivative are nonnegative; setting $g=0$ proves the final stability statement. [step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎
