## Statement

On an oriented tetrahedron $K$ with vertices $x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3$, let $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$ for $0\le i<j\le3$. Then the six edge circulations $\ell_{rs}(v)=\int_{[x_r,x_s]}v\cdot t_{rs}\,ds$ satisfy $\ell_{rs}(\phi_{ij})=\delta_{(r,s),(i,j)}$. The six functions form a basis of the local space $\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:i<j\}=\{a+b\times x:a,b\in\mathbb R^3\}$, so these edge circulations are unisolvent degrees of freedom.

1.1 Parametrize the oriented edge $[x_i,x_j]$ by $x(t)=(1-t)x_i+tx_j$, $0\le t\le1$. Along it, $\lambda_i=1-t$, $\lambda_j=t$, so $\nabla\lambda_j\cdot x'(t)=1$ and $\nabla\lambda_i\cdot x'(t)=-1$. Therefore $\phi_{ij}(x(t))\cdot x'(t)=(1-t)-t(-1)=1$, and $\ell_{ij}(\phi_{ij})=1$. [F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Let $[x_r,x_s]$ be a different edge. If it shares no endpoint with $[x_i,x_j]$, then both $\lambda_i$ and $\lambda_j$ vanish identically along $[x_r,x_s]$, so its circulation is zero. If it shares $x_i$, then $\lambda_j$ vanishes identically along that edge and its directional derivative also vanishes; the remaining term $-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$ is zero. The case sharing $x_j$ is symmetric. Thus $\ell_{rs}(\phi_{ij})=0$ whenever $(r,s)\ne(i,j)$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Each $\phi_{ij}$ is affine in $x$. Its linear part is the skew-symmetric map $x\mapsto(
abla\lambda_i\cdot x)
abla\lambda_j-(
abla\lambda_j\cdot x)
abla\lambda_i$, hence equals $b_{ij}	imes x$ for a unique $b_{ij}\in\mathbb R^3$; its constant part is a vector $a_{ij}$. The space $\{a+b	imes x:a,b\in\mathbb R^3\}$ has dimension six: if $a+b	imes x=0$ on the open tetrahedron, subtracting the values at two points shows $b	imes y=0$ for every $y\in\mathbb R^3$, so $b=0$ and then $a=0$. The six functions are linearly independent because their circulation matrix is the identity by steps 1.1 and 2.1. They therefore form a basis of this six-dimensional space, and the six moments are unisolvent. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Consider an invocation of [[alg-fas-vw-cycle]] on levels $0,\ldots,J$, where
the base solver uses at most $B_0<\infty$ counted operations, every nonlinear
smoother update and residual evaluation returns in finite work, and every
transfer and correction is a finite-dimensional map evaluation. The
invocation terminates with one of its declared statuses. If $W_j$ is the
maximum counted work of a level-$j$ invocation, then
$$W_0\le B_0,\qquad W_j\le C_j+\gamma_jW_{j-1}\quad(1\le j\le J),$$
where $C_j$ is the finite work of that level's pre-smoothing, residual and
transfer evaluations, correction, post-smoothing, and status/diagnostic
bookkeeping. This recurrence counts the actual nonlinear smoother,
coarse-solve, and returned-diagnostic work; it implies no blanket $O(n_J)$
estimate.

1.1 At level $0$, the procedure makes one base-solver call with at most $B_0$ update calls. Each residual evaluation and status check terminates by the given operational assumptions, so the base invocation returns a declared status and $W_0\le B_0$. [given, F1, base]

1.2 A level-$j$ invocation performs its finite pre-smoothing sweeps, one residual and restriction evaluation, and at most $\gamma_j$ calls at level $j-1$. By [A1], each such call terminates with work at most $W_{j-1}$. Recording each returned status, residual, and nested diagnostic list is finite work included in $C_j$. If any call fails, the algorithm returns immediately; otherwise it performs one finite prolongation/correction and its finite post-smoothing sweeps. Thus every branch terminates and its work is at most $C_j+\gamma_jW_{j-1}$. [given, F1, A1, ih, algebra]

2.1 Induction from level $0$ through the finite maximum level $J$ proves termination and the displayed recurrence for every invocation. Early failure only shortens the corresponding counted work. [step 1.1, step 1.2, discharge-induction: step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\|\cdot\|_{DG}$ be the energy expression from [[def-sipdg-bilinear-form-and-energy-norm]] on a finite matching simplicial mesh of a nonempty bounded polyhedral domain, with $\lambda>0$ and $\gamma>0$. Then $\|\cdot\|_{DG}$ is a norm on $V_h^{\rm br}$.

1.1 Suppose $\|v_h\|_{DG}=0$. Every cell-gradient term is zero, and positive definiteness of $A_K$ implies $\nabla(v_h|_K)=0$ almost everywhere. Since $v_h|_K$ is a polynomial on the connected simplex $K$, it is a constant $c_K$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Every interior-facet jump is zero by [F1], so adjacent cells have equal constants. Thus $c_K$ is constant on each connected component of the cell-facet adjacency graph. For any such component, sum [F5] over its finitely many cells. The cell volumes are positive, while the two oriented integrals on every shared facet cancel; if there were no unshared facet, this would give $d\sum_K|K|=0$, a contradiction. Every unshared facet is an exterior mesh facet by the matching property [F2]. On that facet the boundary jump is the cell trace itself, so [F1] forces the component's constant to be zero. Therefore $v_h=0$ on every cell. [F1, F2, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The expression is homogeneous under scalar multiplication. Define its associated pairing by $b_{DG}(v_h,w_h):=\sum_K\int_K
abla v_h^TA_K
abla w_h+\gamma\sum_Fh_F^{-1}\int_F[v_h]_F[w_h]_F$. For any vectors $\xi,\eta$, the quadratic $(\xi+t\eta)^TA_K(\xi+t\eta)$ is nonnegative for all real $t$; if $\eta
e0$, its discriminant is nonpositive, giving $|\xi^TA_K\eta|\le(\xi^TA_K\xi)^{1/2}(\eta^TA_K\eta)^{1/2}$, and the case $\eta=0$ is immediate. [F3] bounds the resulting cell integrals and each facet integral, while [F4] combines the finitely many cell and facet terms to give $|b_{DG}(v_h,w_h)|\le\|v_h\|_{DG}\|w_h\|_{DG}$. Expanding $b_{DG}(v_h+w_h,v_h+w_h)$ gives $\|v_h+w_h\|_{DG}^2\le(\|v_h\|_{DG}+\|w_h\|_{DG})^2$. Thus the triangle inequality holds; together with step 2.1 this proves the norm axioms. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $b_\ell\in\mathcal H_\ell$ for every integer $\ell\ge0$, where $\mathcal H_\ell$ is defined in [[def-spherical-harmonic-partial-wave-conventions]]. Suppose constants $C\ge0$ and $\rho>1$ satisfy $\|b_\ell\|_{L^2(S^2)}\le C\rho^{-\ell}$ for all $\ell$. Then $b(\omega):=\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty b_\ell(\omega)$ converges uniformly on $S^2$, and for every integer $L\ge0$,
$$\sup_{\omega\in S^2}\left|b(\omega)-\sum_{\ell=0}^L b_\ell(\omega)\right|\le C\sqrt{\frac{2L+3}{4\pi}}\,\frac{\rho^{-(L+1)}}{(1-\rho^{-1})^2}.$$
This is a conditional angular-coefficient bound; it does not assert exponential decay for general scattering data.

1.1 By [F1], $\|b_\ell\|_\infty\le C\sqrt{(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)}\rho^{-\ell}$. The scalar series of these bounds converges because $\rho>1$, so the partial sums of $\sum b_\ell$ are uniformly Cauchy and converge uniformly to a function $b$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For $\ell=L+1+n$ with $n\ge0$, $\sqrt{2\ell+1}\le(n+1)\sqrt{2L+3}$: squaring reduces this to $2L+3+2n\le(2L+3)(n+1)^2$, whose difference is nonnegative. Therefore the tail in step 1.1 is at most $C\sqrt{(2L+3)/(4\pi)}\rho^{-(L+1)}\sum_{n=0}^\infty(n+1)\rho^{-n}$. For $t=\rho^{-1}\in(0,1)$, multiplying the geometric series by itself or differentiating its partial sums gives $\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)t^n=(1-t)^{-2}$. This yields the claimed bound. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Write $G_3$ for the Newton kernel of [[def-bem-newtonian-kernel-in-three-dimensions]]. For a smooth density $\lambda$ on $\Gamma$, the classical single-layer potential is
$$S\lambda(x)=\int_\Gamma G_3(x,y)\lambda(y)\,dS_y,\qquad x\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\Gamma.$$

Let $\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ in the norm $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}=\|
abla u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$, using its $L^6$ representative and the trace from [[lem-bem-lipschitz-trace-and-lifting]]. For $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, consider the equation for $u\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}
abla u\cdot
abla v\,dx=\langle\lambda,\gamma vangle_\Gamma\qquad(v\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)).$$
Call such a function a weak single-layer potential and write $S\lambda=u$ when it exists. Define the exterior energy space $E^+(\Omega^+)=\{u\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega^+):u\in L^6(\Omega^+),\ 
abla u\in L^2(\Omega^+)\}$. For a weakly harmonic function $u^-\in H^1(\Omega^-)$, define its weak outward conormal by $\langle\partial_n^-u^-,gangle=\int_{\Omega^-}
abla u^-\cdot
abla L^-g$, where $L^-g$ is any $H^1$ trace lift. For a harmonic $u^+\in E^+(\Omega^+)$, use the same fixed normal $n$ by $\langle\partial_n^+u^+,gangle=-\int_{\Omega^+}
abla u^+\cdot
abla L^+g$ for a compactly supported local lift. In either case the value is independent of the lift: the difference of two lifts has zero trace, and weak harmonicity makes its gradient pairing zero. The exterior formula also gives $\int_{\Omega^+}
abla u^+\cdot
abla v^+=-\langle\partial_n^+u^+,\gamma^+v^+angle$ for every $v^+\in E^+(\Omega^+)$. Indeed, subtract a compactly supported lift of $\gamma^+v^+$; the remaining zero-trace finite-energy function is approximated in gradient norm by compactly supported zero-trace functions using radial cutoffs: $\|v^+
abla\chi_R\|_2\le C\|v^+\|_{L^6(\{R<|x|<2R\})}	o0$. Boundary-chart flattening, zero extension, inward translation, and convolution approximate each zero-trace cutoff by interior smooth tests, so weak harmonicity makes its gradient pairing zero. This proves the energy identity without a flux assumption at infinity. Existence, uniqueness, agreement with the displayed kernel for smooth densities, and the conormal jump are proved in [[thm-bem-single-layer-transmission-mapping-and-coercivity]]. The weak definition fixes the normalization at infinity through $u\in L^6(\mathbb R^3)$; arbitrary additive constants are excluded.

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. Let $a=1/2$ and $g(t)=a\tan(\pi t/4)$. Map the reference square $[-1,1]^2$ to the central square $[-a,a]^2$ by $H(t,q)=(g(t),g(q))$ and split it into two triangles. For the top annular sector use $\theta(t)=\pi/2-\pi t/4$, $r(s,t)=(1-s)a/\sin\theta(t)+s$, and $F(t,s)=r(s,t)(\cos\theta(t),\sin\theta(t))$; split this rectangle into two triangles and rotate it for the other three sides. These ten mapped triangles have positive Jacobians, matching traces, and union equal to the closed unit disk.

1.1 $g'(t)=a(\pi/4)\sec^2(\pi t/4)>0$, so $H$ maps $[-1,1]$ bijectively onto $[-a,a]^2$, since $g(-1)=-a$ and $g(1)=a$. Its Gram determinant gives the same volume factor by [F2]. On the top sector, $\theta'=-\pi/4$ and $r_s=1-a/\sin\theta\ge1-a\sqrt2>0$ because $\sin\theta\ge\sqrt2/2$. Polar-coordinate differentiation gives $\det DF=r r_s(-\theta')>0$; the Gram determinant satisfies $\sqrt{\det(DF^TDF)}=\det DF$. Rotations preserve these determinants. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 At $s=0$, $F(t,0)=(a\cot\theta(t),a)=(g(t),a)$, which is exactly the trace of $H$ on its top edge; at $s=1$, $r=1$, so the outer trace is the unit-circle arc from angle $3\pi/4$ to $\pi/4$. The two radial side traces match those of adjacent rotated sectors. Hence all ten pieces meet only along identical mapped edges. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For each angle $\theta\in[\pi/4,3\pi/4]$, the square boundary on that ray has radius $a/\sin\theta$ and the unit-circle boundary has radius $1$. The sector map covers exactly the radii between them. Four rotated angular ranges cover the annulus outside the central square, with shared corner rays only; $H$ covers the central square. Therefore the ten mapped triangles cover the unit disk without interior overlap. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The central area is $4a^2=1$. By [F3], the sector area is the polar integral $\frac12\int_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4}(1-a^2\csc^2\theta)d\theta$. Since $[-\cot\theta]_{\pi/4}^{3\pi/4}=2$, this equals $\pi/4-a^2=(\pi-1)/4$. Four rotated sectors have total area $\pi-1$, so the union area is $\pi$, consistent with the unit disk. [F3, A1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $A=D\Phi$ and $A_h=D\Phi_h$ be orientation-preserving cell-map derivatives with $\det A,\det A_h\ge j_*>0$, $\|A\|_{op},\|A_h\|_{op}\le M$, and $\|A-A_h\|_{op}\le e_1$. For every unit reference-facet normal $\widehat n$, define the surface Jacobians $J_\Gamma(A)=\|\operatorname{cof}(A)\widehat n\|$, $J_\Gamma(A_h)=\|\operatorname{cof}(A_h)\widehat n\|$, and mapped unit normals $n_\Gamma(A)=\operatorname{cof}(A)\widehat n/J_\Gamma(A)$ and $n_\Gamma(A_h)=\operatorname{cof}(A_h)\widehat n/J_\Gamma(A_h)$. Then
$$\|\operatorname{cof}(A)-\operatorname{cof}(A_h)\|_{op}+|J_\Gamma(A)-J_\Gamma(A_h)|+|n_\Gamma(A)-n_\Gamma(A_h)|\le C(d,M,j_*)e_1.$$
The surface Jacobian agrees with the Gram-metric factor in [[def-isoparametric-curved-cell-map]].

1.1 Each entry of $\operatorname{cof}(A)$ is a signed $(d-1)$-minor, hence a polynomial of degree $d-1$ in the entries of $A$. On the bounded matrix ball $\|A\|_{op},\|A_h\|_{op}\le M$, its derivative is bounded by a constant depending only on $d,M$. The mean-value inequality therefore gives $\|\operatorname{cof}(A)-\operatorname{cof}(A_h)\|_{op}\le C(d,M)\|A-A_h\|_{op}=C(d,M)e_1$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 Let $T$ have orthonormal columns spanning the reference facet tangent space, so $Q=[T,\widehat n]$ is orthogonal. The squared Gram-metric surface factor is $\det(T^TA^TAT)$. The identity $\operatorname{cof}(A)^T\operatorname{cof}(A)=\operatorname{cof}(A^TA)$ and orthogonal covariance of cofactors show $\widehat n^T\operatorname{cof}(A^TA)\widehat n$ is the bottom-right cofactor of $Q^TA^TAQ$, which is exactly $\det(T^TA^TAT)$. Therefore $\|\operatorname{cof}(A)\widehat n\|^2=\det(T^TA^TAT)$, so $J_\Gamma(A)$ is the Gram-metric surface factor. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 If $\sigma_1(A)\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_d(A)>0$ are the singular values, the smallest singular value of $\operatorname{cof}(A)$ is $\prod_{i=2}^d\sigma_i(A)=\det(A)/\sigma_1(A)\ge j_*/M$. Thus $J_\Gamma(A)\ge j_*/M$, and the same bound holds for $A_h$. The reverse triangle inequality and step 1.1 give $|J_\Gamma(A)-J_\Gamma(A_h)|\le C(d,M)e_1$. [F1, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Put $a=\operatorname{cof}(A)\widehat n$ and $b=\operatorname{cof}(A_h)\widehat n$. For nonzero vectors, $|a/|a|-b/|b||\le 2|a-b|/\min(|a|,|b|)$. The lower bounds from step 2.1 and the cofactor gap from step 1.1 therefore imply $|n_\Gamma(A)-n_\Gamma(A_h)|\le C(d,M,j_*)e_1$. Combining the three estimates proves the result. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $A=D\Phi$ and $A_h=D\Phi_h$ be orientation-preserving cell-map derivatives with $\det A,\det A_h\ge j_*>0$, $\|A\|_{op},\|A_h\|_{op}\le M$, and $\|A-A_h\|_{op}\le e_1$. For every unit reference-facet normal $\widehat n$, define the surface Jacobians $J_\Gamma(A)=\|\operatorname{cof}(A)\widehat n\|$, $J_\Gamma(A_h)=\|\operatorname{cof}(A_h)\widehat n\|$, and mapped unit normals $n_\Gamma(A)=\operatorname{cof}(A)\widehat n/J_\Gamma(A)$ and $n_\Gamma(A_h)=\operatorname{cof}(A_h)\widehat n/J_\Gamma(A_h)$. Then
$$\|\operatorname{cof}(A)-\operatorname{cof}(A_h)\|_{op}+|J_\Gamma(A)-J_\Gamma(A_h)|+|n_\Gamma(A)-n_\Gamma(A_h)|\le C(d,M,j_*)e_1.$$
The surface Jacobian agrees with the Gram-metric factor in [[def-isoparametric-curved-cell-map]].

1.1 Each entry of $\operatorname{cof}(A)$ is a signed $(d-1)$-minor, hence a polynomial of degree $d-1$ in the entries of $A$. On the bounded matrix ball $\|A\|_{op},\|A_h\|_{op}\le M$, its derivative is bounded by a constant depending only on $d,M$. The mean-value inequality therefore gives $\|\operatorname{cof}(A)-\operatorname{cof}(A_h)\|_{op}\le C(d,M)\|A-A_h\|_{op}=C(d,M)e_1$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 Let $T$ have orthonormal columns spanning the reference facet tangent space, so $Q=[T,\widehat n]$ is orthogonal. The squared Gram-metric surface factor is $\det(T^TA^TAT)$. The identity $\operatorname{cof}(A)^T\operatorname{cof}(A)=\operatorname{cof}(A^TA)$ and orthogonal covariance of cofactors show $\widehat n^T\operatorname{cof}(A^TA)\widehat n$ is the bottom-right cofactor of $Q^TA^TAQ$, which is exactly $\det(T^TA^TAT)$. Therefore $\|\operatorname{cof}(A)\widehat n\|^2=\det(T^TA^TAT)$, so $J_\Gamma(A)$ is the Gram-metric surface factor. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 If $\sigma_1(A)\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_d(A)>0$ are the singular values, the smallest singular value of $\operatorname{cof}(A)$ is $\prod_{i=2}^d\sigma_i(A)=\det(A)/\sigma_1(A)\ge j_*/M$. Thus $J_\Gamma(A)\ge j_*/M$, and the same bound holds for $A_h$. The reverse triangle inequality and step 1.1 give $|J_\Gamma(A)-J_\Gamma(A_h)|\le C(d,M)e_1$. [F1, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Put $a=\operatorname{cof}(A)\widehat n$ and $b=\operatorname{cof}(A_h)\widehat n$. For nonzero vectors, $|a/|a|-b/|b||\le 2|a-b|/\min(|a|,|b|)$. The lower bounds from step 2.1 and the cofactor gap from step 1.1 therefore imply $|n_\Gamma(A)-n_\Gamma(A_h)|\le C(d,M,j_*)e_1$. Combining the three estimates proves the result. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded polygonal open domain with finite corner set $\mathcal C=\{c_1,\ldots,c_m\}$ and weights $0\le\beta_i<1$. For $\gamma\in[0,\infty)^m$ define $\Phi_\gamma(x)=\prod_i|x-c_i|^{\gamma_i}$; $\beta+j-2$ means componentwise addition. For integer $k\ge2$, define

$$
\|v\|_{H^{k,2}_\beta(\Omega)}^2=\|v\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2+\sum_{j=2}^k\sum_{|\alpha|=j}\|\Phi_{\beta+j-2}D^\alpha v\|_2^2.
$$

Let $B^2_\beta(\Omega)$ consist of real-valued functions in every $H^{k,2}_\beta(\Omega)$ for which some $C_u,d_u>0$ satisfy

$$
\left\|\Phi_{\beta+k-2}\sum_{|\alpha|=k}|D^\alpha u|\right\|_2\le C_ud_u^{k-2}(k-2)!\qquad(k\ge2).
$$

Let $(\mathcal T_k)_{k\ge1}$ be nested finite matching shape-regular affine triangulations of $\Omega$, with at most $C_0k$ triangles. Write $h_T=\operatorname{diam}(T)$ and $\operatorname{dist}(T,\mathcal C)=\inf_{x\in T,c\in\mathcal C}|x-c|$. Assume a fixed $0<\sigma<1$ and $C_1>0$ satisfy

$$
\sigma\le\frac{h_T}{\operatorname{dist}(T,\mathcal C)}\le\sigma^{-1}\quad(\overline T\cap\mathcal C=\varnothing),\qquad h_T\le C_1\sigma^k\quad(\overline T\cap\mathcal C\ne\varnothing).
$$

Let $p_k\in\mathbb N$ be uniform total polynomial degrees with $c_0k\le p_k\le c_1k$ for fixed $0<c_0\le c_1$. For a fixed union $\Gamma_D$ of polygon edges, let $V_k$ be the space of broken piecewise-$\mathbb P_{p_k}$ functions whose polynomial traces agree on every interior edge and vanish on the boundary edges in $\Gamma_D$; put $N_k=\dim V_k$. This is the corresponding subspace of the variable-degree space in [[def-hp-variable-degree-spaces-on-matching-meshes]].
For this smoother class, the boundary condition means that the unique continuous representative supplied by [[lem-hp-weighted-analytic-corner-pointwise-control]] vanishes pointwise on the edges in $\Gamma_D$; no zero condition is imposed on the other edges. If $u\in B^2_\beta(\Omega)$ satisfies this boundary condition, then constants $C,b>0$, independent of $k$, satisfy

$$
\inf_{v_k\in V_k}\|\nabla(u-v_k)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le Ce^{-bN_k^{1/3}}.
$$

For a bounded coercive conforming Galerkin problem on a Hilbert space $V\subset H^1(\Omega)$ containing $u$, with $V_k\subset V$ and norm equivalent to the gradient seminorm on $V$, Céa's estimate gives the same exponential rate for the energy error, with its actual $M/\alpha$ and norm-equivalence factors included. The constants may depend on the polygon, weights, weighted analytic bounds, mesh shape and grading constants, degree constants, $\Gamma_D$, and the Galerkin coercivity and norm-equivalence constants.

1.1 Fix $0<a<\min_i(1-\beta_i)$ as in [F1]. Call a cell a cap when its closure contains a corner. Since the corner set is finite and distinct corners have positive separation, for all sufficiently large $k$ each cap contains at most one corner; its diameter is at most $C_1\sigma^k$. On a noncap cell $T$ with $d_T=\operatorname{dist}(T,\mathcal C)<R$, the mesh condition gives $\sigma\le h_T/d_T\le\sigma^{-1}$, so [F1] gives uniform scaled analytic derivative bounds after subtracting a suitable constant. If $d_T\ge R$, the compact-away-from-corners bounds in [F1], together with bounded $h_T$ and the fixed $r_T=R$, give the same conclusion after enlarging constants. Thus each noncap reference pullback has derivative bounds $C r_T^a A_1^{|\alpha|}|\alpha|!$, where $r_T=\min(R,d_T)$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For every mesh edge incident to a polygon corner, prescribe the linear interpolant of the two endpoint values of the continuous representative of $u$. All cells sharing such an edge are caps. On every other edge $E$, prescribe the single common endpoint-preserving derivative-projection polynomial $g_E$ from [F2], in one globally fixed edge orientation. The edge lies a distance comparable to its length from any nearby corner: for an edge opposite a cap corner this follows from shape regularity and the altitude bound, and for a noncap neighbor it also follows from the mesh ratio condition. Thus [F1]–[F2] give, on each noncap edge, $\|u-g_E\|_{L^\infty(E)}+\ell_E^{1/2}\|\partial_\tau(u-g_E)\|_{L^2(E)}\le C r_T^a e^{-bp_k}$ for each adjoining noncap cell, with comparable scales on both sides. Here the sup bound follows from the endpoint identity and $\|e\|_\infty\le\|e'\|_{L^1}\le\|e'\|_{L^2}$ for the endpoint-zero reference error; [F6] justifies the last inequality. On an edge incident to a corner, both adjacent cells are caps, its prescribed linear polynomial shares the exact continuous vertex values, and no tangential regularity of $u$ at the corner is used. Every edge polynomial takes the value of $u$ at both endpoints. If $E\subset\Gamma_D$, these endpoint values and the entire prescribed edge polynomial are zero. [F1, F2, F6, step 1.1, given, construct]

3.1 Let $T$ be a noncap triangle and choose $q_T\in\mathbb P_{p_k}(T)$ by transporting the analytic approximation [F2] for the scaled pullback, then adding back its subtracted constant. Thus $\|u-q_T\|_\infty+h_T\|\nabla(u-q_T)\|_\infty\le Cr_T^ae^{-bp_k}$. Correct its three vertex values by an affine polynomial to obtain $\widetilde q_T$ matching the prescribed $g_E$ at all vertices; the correction has $H^1$ seminorm at most $Cr_T^ae^{-bp_k}$. On each edge, $g_E-\widetilde q_T|_E$ has zero endpoints, degree at most $p_k$, and strong edge derivative norm at most $Cr_T^ae^{-bp_k}$. Lift these three residuals separately by [F3]. Their sum does not change the other edge traces, so the resulting $v_T\in\mathbb P_{p_k}(T)$ has all three prescribed traces and $|u-v_T|_{H^1(T)}\le Cr_T^ae^{-bp_k}\le Ce^{-bp_k}.$ [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Let $T$ be a cap at corner $c_i$, with diameter $h_T$; for large $k$ it contains no other corner. Start with the affine interpolant $a_T$ of the three exact vertex values. By [F1], $|u-a_T|_{H^1(T)}\le Ch_T^a$. Its two edges incident to $c_i$ already have the prescribed linear traces. On the opposite edge $E$, every point has distance comparable to $h_T$ from $c_i$, so the gradient bound in [F1] and Cauchy–Schwarz [F6] give $\ell_E^{1/2}\|\partial_\tau u\|_{L^2(E)}\le Ch_T^a$. The interval derivative projection in [F2] is contractive, and the vertex estimate in [F1] gives the same bound for $g_E-a_T|_E$. This discrepancy vanishes at both endpoints; add its lift from [F3]. The resulting polynomial has all prescribed traces and $|u-v_T|_{H^1(T)}\le Ch_T^a\le C\sigma^{ak}$. No $H^2$ regularity is used on a cap. [F1, F2, F3, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Every pair of adjacent local polynomials has common trace $g_E$; the boundary traces vanish on $\Gamma_D$. Thus they assemble to $v_k\in V_k$ by [F4]. Summing squared cell errors from steps 3.1 and 3.2 over at most $C_0k$ cells gives $\|\nabla(u-v_k)\|_2\le C\sqrt{k}\left(e^{-bp_k}+\sigma^{ak}\right)\le C'e^{-\eta k}$ for some $\eta>0$, because $p_k\ge c_0k$ and $0<\sigma<1$. The finitely many earlier meshes are handled by $v_k=0$ and an increase of $C'$. Since $N_k\le C_Nk^3$ by [F4], $k\ge C_N^{-1/3}N_k^{1/3}$ and therefore $\inf_{v\in V_k}\|\nabla(u-v)\|_2\le C e^{-bN_k^{1/3}}$. [F4, step 3.1, step 3.2, given, algebra]

5.1 Let $V$ and its Galerkin form satisfy the additional hypotheses in the statement. Apply Céa [F5] to the best-approximation estimate of step 4.1. Norm equivalence between $\|\cdot\|_V$ and the gradient seminorm changes only the stated constant, and the actual $M/\alpha$ factor is retained. This proves the energy-error conclusion. [F5, step 4.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $A$ be a nonempty finite ordered control set.
For each $a\in A$ and $j=1,\ldots,d$, let
$\alpha_j^a,b_j^a,f^a:\mathbb T^d\times[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and
periodic, jointly continuous in $(x,t)$, and uniformly Lipschitz in $(x,t)$.
Assume a common constant $\alpha_*>0$ satisfies
$$\alpha_j^a(x,t)\ge\alpha_*\qquad\text{for every }a,j,x,t.$$
The **diagonal controlled-diffusion HJB Cauchy problem** is
$$u_t-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(\alpha_j^a(x,t)u_{x_jx_j}+b_j^a(x,t)u_{x_j}\bigr)+f^a(x,t) \right\}=0\quad\text{on }\mathbb T^d\times(0,T),$$
with continuous periodic initial data $u(x,0)=u_0(x)$. In the convention
$u_t+F(x,t,Du,D^2u)=0$, this has
$$F(x,t,p,X)=-\max_{a\in A}\left\{ \sum_j(\alpha_j^a X_{jj}+b_j^a p_j)+f^a\right\},$$
which is nonincreasing in each diagonal Hessian entry. No off-diagonal
diffusion or arbitrary anisotropic central stencil is covered.

## Definition

Let $b=(\tau,\sigma)$ be an admissible leaf of the finite block-cluster partition in [[def-hlr-and-h2-block-matrix-representations]]. A **factor-sum tree for $b$** is a finite rooted binary tree whose leaves carry factor pairs $U_v\in\mathbb F^{\tau\times r_v}$, $V_v\in\mathbb F^{\sigma\times r_v}$ for exact contributions $M_v=U_vV_v^*$; each internal node denotes the sum of the exact matrices denoted by its two children. Here $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $*$ is conjugate transpose, and all factors have the displayed finite dimensions.

**Input:** Such a tree, a rank cap $k\ge1$, node tolerances $\theta_v\ge0$ whose sum over all nodes is at most a requested block tolerance $\delta_b\ge0$, and the procedures/results [[alg-hlr-core-svd-recompression-with-tolerance]] and [[thm-hlr-core-svd-recompression-is-best-rank-tolerance]].

**Procedure:** Traverse the tree in postorder. At a leaf, pass its exact factor pair to core-SVD recompression. At an internal node, concatenate the returned child factor pairs, which represents the sum of the two child approximations, and pass that pair to core-SVD recompression. At every node use effective core cap $k_b=\min(k,|\tau|,|\sigma|)$ and tolerance $\theta_v$. If any call returns **tolerance-not-met**, return that status and node. On success, retain its factors and exact discarded-tail norm $\rho_v$. Define the node's reported error bound by $e_v=\rho_v$ at a leaf and $e_v=e_{v_1}+e_{v_2}+\rho_v$ at an internal node. If all calls succeed, return the root factors and $e_{\rm root}$. Then the root matrix has rank at most $k$ and its Frobenius error from the sum of all leaf contributions is at most $e_{\rm root}\le\sum_v\theta_v\le\delta_b$. A failed call means only that this chosen tree and its assigned local budgets did not produce a certificate; it does not assert that no rank-$k$ approximation of the full sum meets $\delta_b$.

Near blocks are not passed to this routine: they are assembled and stored densely and exactly. For a leaf carrying a dense contribution $D\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, use the exact factor pair $(D,I_n)$, where $I_n$ is the identity matrix; the routine may then compress it under its assigned tolerance.

The rank and error guarantees are proved in [[lem-hlr-bottom-up-recompression-error-bound]].

A **factor-sum tree for $b$** is a finite rooted binary tree whose leaves carry factor pairs $U_v\in\mathbb F^{\tau\times r_v}$, $V_v\in\mathbb F^{\sigma\times r_v}$ for exact contributions $M_v=U_vV_v^*$; each internal node denotes the sum of the exact matrices denoted by its two children. Here $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $*$ is conjugate transpose, and all factors have the displayed finite dimensions.

**Procedure:** Traverse the tree in postorder. At a leaf, pass its exact factor pair to core-SVD recompression. At an internal node, concatenate the returned child factor pairs, which represents the sum of the two child approximations, and pass that pair to core-SVD recompression. At every node use effective core cap $k_b=\min(k,|\tau|,|\sigma|)$ and tolerance $\theta_v$. If any call returns **tolerance-not-met**, return that status and node. On success, retain its factors and exact discarded-tail norm $\rho_v$. Define the node's reported error bound by $e_v=\rho_v$ at a leaf and $e_v=e_{v_1}+e_{v_2}+\rho_v$ at an internal node. Then the root matrix has rank at most $k$ and its Frobenius error from the sum of all leaf contributions is at most $e_{\rm root}\le\sum_v\theta_v\le\delta_b$. For a leaf carrying a dense contribution $D\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, use the exact factor pair $(D,I_n)$, where $I_n$ is the identity matrix; the routine may then compress it under its assigned tolerance.

## Example

Let $\tau=\{1,2\}$ have coordinates $0$ and $1$, choose leaf threshold $b=2$, and use the block $\tau\times\tau$. Its distance from itself is zero, so it is inadmissible and terminates as a dense near block. For $I_2$, no rank-one approximation has operator-norm error below one.

1.1 Since $\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\tau)=0$, $(\tau,\tau)$ is not admissible. The cluster has size $b$ and is a leaf, so its block pair is terminal and near by [F1]; [F2] therefore stores this block densely. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The singular values of $I_2$ are $1,1$. Applying [F3] with rank cap one shows $\|I_2-B\|_2\ge1$ for every rank-at-most-one $B$, where [F4] identifies this norm as the maximum unit-vector stretch. Thus a rank-one far-block representation cannot meet any spectral error tolerance strictly below one. [given, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $X\succeq0$ be the stabilizing CARE solution from [[thm-care-stabilizing-psd-solution-and-value]], let $G=BR^{-1}B^*$, and define
$$H=\begin{bmatrix}A&-G\\-Q&-A^*\end{bmatrix},\qquad A_c=A-GX.$$
Then
$$H\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}A_c.$$
Moreover, $H$ has exactly $n$ eigenvalues in the open left half-plane and $n$ in the open right half-plane, none on the imaginary axis, and $\operatorname{Ran}\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}$ is its stable invariant subspace.
1.1 Block multiplication gives $H\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}A-GX\\-Q-A^*X\end{bmatrix}.$ By [F1], $-Q-A^*X=XA-XGX=X(A-GX)$, proving the graph identity. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Set $T_X=\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\X&I\end{bmatrix}$, whose inverse is $\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\-X&I\end{bmatrix}$. Using [F1], $T_X^{-1}HT_X=\begin{bmatrix}A-GX&-G\\0&-(A-GX)^*\end{bmatrix}.$ The eigenvalues of the first diagonal block lie in the open left half-plane by [F1]. If $\lambda$ is a root of its characteristic polynomial, then $-\overline\lambda$ is a root of the characteristic polynomial of $-(A-GX)^*$, since $\det(-\overline\lambda I+(A-GX)^*)=\overline{\det(-\lambda I+(A-GX))}=0$; these reflected roots lie in the open right half-plane. By [F5] each diagonal characteristic polynomial has degree $n$ and splits into $n$ roots counted with algebraic multiplicity. The characteristic polynomial factorization [F3] and root/eigenvalue connection [F4] therefore give exactly $n$ eigenvalues of $H$ in each open half-plane and none on the imaginary axis.  The first coordinate subspace is invariant and its restriction has the stable spectrum of $A-GX$. Any generalized eigenvector of the displayed triangular matrix for a stable eigenvalue has trailing component in the kernel of a power of $(-(A-GX)^* -\lambda I)$; that matrix is invertible because the trailing spectrum is in the open right half-plane, so the trailing component is zero. By [F6] these generalized eigenspaces have total dimension equal to the stable algebraic multiplicity $n$ from [F5], so they fill the first coordinate subspace, which is therefore the stable invariant subspace. Applying $T_X$ maps it to $\operatorname{Ran}\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $r_i$ be linearly degenerate on a neighborhood and let $R_i(\sigma;u_0)$
be its local rarefaction curve. Then the states $u_0$ and
$u_1=R_i(\sigma;u_0)$ are joined by a Rankine–Hugoniot jump of speed
$\lambda_i(u_0)$, and the corresponding moving discontinuity is a weak
solution. The characteristic speed is equal on the two sides; this is a
contact wave, not a strict Lax shock.

1.1 Along the curve, the chain rule gives $\frac{d}{d\sigma}\lambda_i(R_i(\sigma;u_0))=D\lambda_i(R_i)r_i(R_i)=0$, so $\lambda_i(R_i)=\lambda_i(u_0)$. Also $\frac{d}{d\sigma}f(R_i)=Df(R_i)r_i(R_i)=\lambda_i(u_0)r_i(R_i)$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Integrating the second identity from $0$ to $\sigma$ yields $f(u_1)-f(u_0)=\lambda_i(u_0)(u_1-u_0)$, the Rankine–Hugoniot equality [F3]. Applying [F4] gives the weak moving contact wave; equality of the characteristic speed on both sides was proved in step 1.1. [step 1.1, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U$ be bounded and open, $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, and $\rho>0$. For every $\xi\in\mathbb R^d$ and coordinate $j$,
$$\int_0^\infty2\pi|\xi_j||\widehat\phi(t\xi)|dt\le \rho^{-1}\|\phi\|_1+\rho\|\partial_j^2\phi\|_1.$$
If $T_{\phi,j}$ is the distributional operator of [[lem-na-bogovskii-truncated-derivative-fourier-formula]], then for every $f\in C_c^\infty(U)$ its restriction to $U$ is in $L^2(U)$ and
$$\|T_{\phi,j}f\|_{L^2(U)}\le A_j(\phi)\|f\|_{L^2(U)},\quad A_j(\phi)=2^{(d-1)/2}(\rho^{-1}\|\phi\|_1+\rho\|\partial_j^2\phi\|_1)+2^d|U|\|\partial_j\phi\|_\infty.$$
By density, this restriction has a unique bounded extension $L^2(U)\to L^2(U)$ with the same bound.

1.1 If $\xi_j=0$, the left side of the ray estimate is zero. Otherwise put $t_0=(2\pi\rho|\xi_j|)^{-1}$. On $[0,t_0]$, use $|\widehat\phi|\le\|\phi\|_1$ to bound the integral by $2\pi|\xi_j|t_0\|\phi\|_1=\rho^{-1}\|\phi\|_1$. [given, algebra]

2.1 On $[t_0,\infty)$, [F2] gives $|\widehat\phi(t\xi)|\le(4\pi^2t^2\xi_j^2)^{-1}\|\partial_j^2\phi\|_1$. Integrating $2\pi|\xi_j|t^{-2}/(4\pi^2\xi_j^2)$ from $t_0$ to infinity gives $\rho\|\partial_j^2\phi\|_1$. Adding the intervals proves the ray bound. [A1, F2, algebra, step 1.1]

3.1 Write $m(t,\xi)=2\pi|\xi_j||\widehat\phi(t\xi)|$. Cauchy–Schwarz in $t$ and step 2.1 yield $|\widehat{T^<f}(\xi)|^2\le R_j(\phi)\int_0^{1/2}m(t,\xi)|\widehat f((1-t)\xi)|^2dt,$ where $R_j(\phi)=\rho^{-1}\|\phi\|_1+\rho\|\partial_j^2\phi\|_1$. Integrate in $\xi$, set $\eta=(1-t)\xi$, and then $s=t/(1-t)$. Since $(1-t)^{-(d+1)}dt=(1+s)^{d-1}ds\le2^{d-1}ds$ for $0\le s\le1$, the inner integral is at most $2^{d-1}R_j(\phi)\|f\|_2^2$ by the ray bound and [F2]. Plancherel [F2] then gives $\|T^<_{\phi,j}f\|_2\le2^{(d-1)/2}R_j(\phi)\|f\|_2$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 For $1/2\le t\le1$, the kernel $t^{-d}\partial_{x_j}[\phi(y+(x-y)/t)]$ has absolute value at most $2^{d+1}\|\partial_j\phi\|_\infty$; integrating the sharper factor $t^{-d-1}$ over this interval gives at most $2^d\|\partial_j\phi\|_\infty$. On $U\times U$ its integral operator has $L^2(U)$ norm at most $2^d|U|\|\partial_j\phi\|_\infty$ by Cauchy–Schwarz in $y$ and then $x$. Add this to the short-range bound of step 3.1, which was proved on all of $\mathbb R^d$ and hence also holds after restriction to $U$. [A1, F1, given, F4, step 3.1]

5.1 The estimates hold first for $f\in C_c^\infty(U)$. Density in $L^2(U)$ extends the restriction of the distributional operator uniquely to all $L^2(U)$ inputs and preserves the same bound. Convergence in $L^2(U)$ implies convergence against every test function in $C_c^\infty(U)$, so this extension agrees on $U$ with the distributional limit from the definition. [A1, F1, F3, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$. If $d=1$, let the cells be a finite oriented interval mesh from [[def-pe04-one-dimensional-interval-mesh-and-broken-polynomials]]; if $d\ge2$, let them form a finite matching affine simplicial mesh. On every cell assume diagonal-norm SBP data of [[def-pe04-diagonal-norm-sbp-element-data]], with paired interior face nodes, equal paired weights, and opposite outward normals. Let $\beta\in\mathbb R^d$ be constant, and let the differentiable nodal state $U_K(t)$ solve the upwind SBP-SAT method of [[def-pe04-upwind-sbp-sat-transport-discretization]] with prescribed inflow values $g_{F,q}$ where $b_{K,F}:=\beta\cdot n_{K,F}<0$. Write $\omega_{F,q}$ for the diagonal entries of the face norm. On an interior face oriented from $K^-$ to $K^+$, set $b_F=\beta\cdot n_F$ and $[U]_{F,q}=U^+_{F,q}-U^-_{F,q}$. Let $\Gamma_+$ and $\Gamma_-$ denote the boundary faces with positive and negative outward speed, respectively. For $d=1$, each face has one endpoint node and its face sum is a one-point sum. The discrete energy $E_h=\frac12\sum_K U_K^TH_KU_K$ satisfies
$$\frac{dE_h}{dt}+\frac12\sum_{F\text{ interior}}\sum_q\omega_{F,q}|b_F|[U]_{F,q}^2+\frac12\sum_{F\subset\Gamma_+}\sum_q\omega_{F,q}b_{K,F}U_{F,q}^2+\frac12\sum_{F\subset\Gamma_-}\sum_q\omega_{F,q}|b_{K,F}|(U_{F,q}-g_{F,q})^2=\frac12\sum_{F\subset\Gamma_-}\sum_q\omega_{F,q}|b_{K,F}|g_{F,q}^2.$$
Consequently, zero inflow data give a nonincreasing SBP norm.

1.1 Multiply the cell equation in [F2] on the left by $U_K^T$. The derivative term is $\frac12\frac{d}{dt}(U_K^TH_KU_K)$ because $H_K$ is symmetric. For each direction, the scalar identity $U_K^TQ_{K,\ell}U_K=\frac12U_K^T(Q_{K,\ell}+Q_{K,\ell}^T)U_K$ and [F1] give the face contribution $\frac12\sum_F b_{K,F}U_{K,F}^TM_{K,F}U_{K,F}$ after summing with coefficients $\beta_\ell$. Including the SAT term, the cell energy equation is
$$\frac12\frac{d}{dt}(U_K^TH_KU_K)+\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\left(b_{K,F}\widehat U_{K,F}^TM_{K,F}U_{K,F}-\frac{b_{K,F}}2U_{K,F}^TM_{K,F}U_{K,F}\right)=0.$$
[F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Fix an interior face oriented from $K^-$ to $K^+$ and a paired node $q$. Its paired face weights are equal by [F1]. If $b_F>0$, both upwind traces are $U^-_{F,q}$, so the two contributions in step 1.1 sum to $\frac{\omega_{F,q}b_F}{2}(U^-_{F,q}-U^+_{F,q})^2$. If $b_F<0$, the upwind traces are $U^+_{F,q}$ and the sum is $\frac{\omega_{F,q}|b_F|}{2}(U^+_{F,q}-U^-_{F,q})^2$. If $b_F=0$, both contributions vanish. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 At a boundary face with $b_{K,F}>0$, $\widehat U_{K,F}=U_{K,F}$, so each node contributes $\omega_{F,q}b_{K,F}U_{F,q}^2/2$. When $b_{K,F}<0$, $\widehat U_{K,F}=g_{F,q}$, so the contribution is $\omega_{F,q}|b_{K,F}|(U_{F,q}-g_{F,q})^2/2-\omega_{F,q}|b_{K,F}|g_{F,q}^2/2$. Zero-speed faces contribute zero. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Sum the contributions from steps 2.1 and 2.2 over all cells. Each paired interior node appears once in the jump sum, and boundary nodes appear once in the corresponding inflow or outflow sum, yielding the displayed identity. Positivity of the face weights makes every dissipation term nonnegative; hence zero inflow data imply $dE_h/dt\le0$. [given, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Take five periodic cells, $g=1$, bed values $(b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4)=(0,1,2,1,0)$, and free-surface level $\eta_0=2$. Set $m_i=0$ and $h_i=(2-b_i)_+$, so $(h_i)=(2,1,0,1,2)$; the crest cell is dry.

1.1 The data are admissible by [F1]. The four face maxima, including the periodic face between cells $4$ and $0$, are $(1,2,2,1,0)$, so the paired reconstructed depths are respectively $(1,1)$, $(0,0)$, $(0,0)$, $(1,1)$, and $(2,2)$. All reconstructed velocities are zero. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 At these equal states the common HLL fluxes are $(0,1/2)$, $(0,0)$, $(0,0)$, $(0,1/2)$ and $(0,2)$. Adding the one-sided pressure corrections in [F2] makes the two corrected fluxes adjacent to each cell both equal $(0,h_i^2/2)$: the five cell pressures are $2,1/2,0,1/2,2$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Each cell therefore has zero corrected-flux difference in the update, so every state is unchanged, including the dry crest. This verifies the exact lake-at-rest preservation in [F3] for this finite wet/dry example. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Take five periodic cells, $g=1$, bed values $(b_0,b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4)=(0,1,2,1,0)$, and free-surface level $\eta_0=2$. Set $m_i=0$ and $h_i=(2-b_i)_+$, so $(h_i)=(2,1,0,1,2)$; the crest cell is dry.

1.1 The data are admissible by [F1]. The four face maxima, including the periodic face between cells $4$ and $0$, are $(1,2,2,1,0)$, so the paired reconstructed depths are respectively $(1,1)$, $(0,0)$, $(0,0)$, $(1,1)$, and $(2,2)$. All reconstructed velocities are zero. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 At these equal states the common HLL fluxes are $(0,1/2)$, $(0,0)$, $(0,0)$, $(0,1/2)$ and $(0,2)$. Adding the one-sided pressure corrections in [F2] makes the two corrected fluxes adjacent to each cell both equal $(0,h_i^2/2)$: the five cell pressures are $2,1/2,0,1/2,2$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Each cell therefore has zero corrected-flux difference in the update, so every state is unchanged, including the dry crest. This verifies the exact lake-at-rest preservation in [F3] for this finite wet/dry example. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded connected open set whose
boundary is locally the graph of a Lipschitz function (a bounded Lipschitz
domain). The zero-tangential boundary condition is the perfect-electric-
conductor (PEC) condition. We use PEC to name the closure convention below;
for a smooth field this is the usual condition $n\times u=0$ on the boundary.
Its space is
$$V:=H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega),$$
with the graph norm and closure convention of
[[def-na-hcurl-space]] and [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]. For a positive
constant permittivity $\epsilon$ and a positive constant permeability $\mu$,
write
$$(u,v)_\epsilon:=\epsilon\int_\Omega u\cdot v\,dx,\qquad K:=\{u\in V:\operatorname{curl}u=0\},\qquad X:=V\cap K^{\perp_\epsilon}.$$
Thus $X$ removes the entire PEC curl kernel, without identifying that kernel
with a scalar gradient range.

For a bounded polyhedral subcase with a finite matching affine tetrahedral
mesh $\mathcal T_h$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], let
$$V_h:=N_h^1\cap V,\qquad K_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:\operatorname{curl}v_h=0\},\qquad X_h:=V_h\cap K_h^{\perp_\epsilon},$$
where $N_h^1$ is the lowest-order first-family edge space of
[[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. The notation for $K_h$ and
the $L^2$ quotient gauge follows [[def-na-curl-curl-kernel-quotient-gauge]],
restricted to this PEC subspace. The continuous PEC eigenproblem
is to find $\lambda>0$ and $0\ne u\in X$ such that
$$\mu^{-1}(\operatorname{curl}u,\operatorname{curl}v)_{L^2} =\lambda (u,v)_\epsilon\qquad(v\in X).$$
The discrete problem replaces $X$ by $X_h$ and tests against every $v_h\in X_h$.
The unquotiented PEC pencil on $V$ is to find $\lambda\ge0$ and
$0\ne u\in V$ such that the same weak equation holds for every $v\in V$.
The positive constants are homogeneous scalar coefficients. The coefficient
extensions to variable or tensor-valued media require their own weighted
compactness hypotheses and are not inferred from the unweighted PE09
discrete-compactness interface.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice, $d\ge2$, a nonempty connected bounded polyhedral open set $\Omega$, a finite matching shape-regular affine simplicial mesh $\mathcal T_h$, and a polynomial degree $k\ge1$ as in [[def-nitsche-boundary-penalty-forms]]. Put $h:=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}h_K$ and $\ell_\Omega:=\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)$. For every $1/2<s\le1$ there is an explicitly defined linear map
$$I_{h,0}:H^{1+s}(\Omega)\cap H^1_0(\Omega)\longrightarrow \mathbb P_1(\mathcal T_h)\cap H^1_0(\Omega)\subseteq Y_h$$
such that
$$\|\zeta-I_{h,0}\zeta\|_{\#,h}\le C h^s\|\zeta\|_{H^{1+s}(\Omega)}=C_D h^s\ell_\Omega^{1-s}\|\zeta\|_{H^{1+s}(\Omega)},\qquad C_D:=C\ell_\Omega^{s-1}.$$
Here $\|\cdot\|_{\#,h}$ and $Y_h=V_h\cap H^1_0(\Omega)$ are exactly those of [[def-nitsche-boundary-penalty-forms]]. The constants are uniform over the mesh family and depend only on $d,s$ and its shape-regularity bound; the displayed conversion to $C_D$ uses the fixed nonempty domain. The construction uses cell means and affine reconstructions, never point values of $\zeta$. Its boundary-value error vanishes exactly. No approximation statement for higher polynomial degree or for nonzero-trace primal data is asserted.

1.1 For each cell $K$, let $b_K$ be its centroid, let $m_K:=|K|^{-1}\int_K\zeta$, and let $g_K:=|K|^{-1}\int_K
abla\zeta$. Define the affine polynomial $p_K(x):=m_K+g_K\cdot(x-b_K)$ and set $A_K:=|
abla\zeta|_{s,K}$, where at $s=1$ this is the cell $L^2$ norm of the weak Hessian. The mean of $\zeta-p_K$ is zero and the mean of its gradient is zero. The mean-zero fractional Poincaré estimate [F2] applied to $
abla\zeta$ gives $\|
abla(\zeta-p_K)\|_K\le C h_K^sA_K$; ordinary mean-zero Poincaré applied to $\zeta-p_K$ then gives $\|\zeta-p_K\|_K\le C h_K^{1+s}A_K$. [F1, F2, given]

1.2 We record the required vertex-star geometry. The solid angle of every shape-regular cell at any vertex is at least $c(d,\sigma)>0$: the inscribed ball has radius at least $h_K/\sigma$, its center is at distance at most $h_K$ from the vertex, and rays through that ball contain a spherical cap of radius bounded below in terms of $\sigma$. Disjoint cell interiors give disjoint solid-angle interiors, so at most $N(d,\sigma)$ cells meet at a vertex. In the spherical link of a vertex, facet adjacency is adjacency of cells across a facet containing that vertex. At an interior vertex the link is the full sphere. Its cell-adjacency graph is connected: for $d=2$ the link is a circle divided into arcs; for $d\ge3$, each codimension-two-or-higher link face has dimension at most $d-3$, and the directions of endpoints whose chord from a fixed generic direction meets that face lie in its radial cone, of spherical dimension at most $d-2<d-1$. A finite union of these forbidden sets has measure zero, so choose an intermediate direction outside the forbidden sets for two generic endpoints and join them by two projected chord segments. The resulting path avoids the lower-dimensional skeleton and crosses only facet interiors, proving graph connectivity. At a boundary vertex, every connected component of the graph contains a boundary facet incident to the vertex. Otherwise a path from a cell-interior direction in that component to any generic direction cannot leave the component: each crossing is through a link facet, and the assumed absence of an exposed facet gives a neighboring cell in the same component. Thus every generic direction belongs to that component; its finite closed link is the full sphere, and the finitely many incident simplices then contain a whole ball about the vertex, making it interior, a contradiction. Any shortest path in a component has at most $N-1$ edges; shape regularity makes diameters comparable across each shared facet, so all cells on such a path have diameters comparable by a uniform constant. [F3, given, choose]

2.1 Apply [F2] with exponent $1$ to $\zeta-p_K$ and use step 1.1. This yields $\|T_F(\zeta-p_K)\|_F\le C h_K^{s+1/2}A_K$. Apply [F2] with exponent $s$ to each component of $\nabla(\zeta-p_K)$; its cell $L^2$ norm is bounded by step 1.1 and its fractional seminorm equals $A_K$ for $s<1$, while at $s=1$ its weak derivative is the Hessian. Thus $h_K^{1/2}\|T_F\nabla(\zeta-p_K)\|_F\le C h_K^sA_K$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For an interior mesh vertex $z$, define $c_z$ as the arithmetic mean of $p_L(z)$ over all incident cells $L$; for a boundary vertex set $c_z:=0$. Let $I_{h,0}\zeta$ be the continuous piecewise-affine function with these nodal coefficients. We prove that the cell traces of the global $H^1(\Omega)$ function $\zeta$ agree across each interior facet $F$. Exhaust the relative interior of $F$ by the compact sets $E_m:=\{x\in F:\operatorname{dist}_F(x,\partial F)\ge1/m\}$, omitting empty sets; each lies in $F\cap\Omega$ by the matching-mesh convention, and the omitted facet rim has surface measure zero. Fix $E_m$ and choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ equal to one on a neighborhood of $E_m$, using [F8]. Then $v:=\chi\zeta\in W^{1,2}(\Omega)$ has compact support, and its zero extension $V$ lies in $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^d)$ by [F8]. Choose a nonnegative smooth unit-mass mollifier $\rho$ supported in the unit ball and put $V_\varepsilon=\rho_\varepsilon*V$. For every $q\in L^2(\mathbb R^d)$, change variables in the convolution integral and apply scalar Jensen and Tonelli as in [F9] to get $\|\rho_\varepsilon*q-q\|_2^2\le\int\rho_\varepsilon(a)\|\tau_{-a}q-q\|_2^2\,da\le\sup_{|a|\le\varepsilon}\|\tau_{-a}q-q\|_2^2\to0$. Apply this to $q=V$ and to each weak first derivative of $V$; the weak-derivative commutation in [F9] proves $V_\varepsilon\to V$ in $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^d)$. The cell trace maps are local on $E_m$: if two $W^{1,2}(K)$ functions agree in a neighborhood of $E_m$, their difference $w$ is zero there; for any compact subpatch $E\subset E_m$, choose a smooth cutoff $\eta$ supported in that neighborhood and equal to one near $E$. By [F10] choose smooth functions $w_j\to w$ in $W^{1,2}(K)$. Weak multiplication and the trace estimate show $\eta w_j\to0$ in $W^{1,2}(K)$ and $T_F(\eta w_j)=\eta|_F w_j|_F\to0$ in $L^2(F)$; also $\eta|_Fw_j|_F\to\eta|_FT_Fw$ by trace continuity. Since $\eta=1$ on $E$, $T_Fw=0$ there. Exhausting $E_m$ by compact subpatches proves locality on $E_m$. Thus $V$ and $\zeta$ have the same traces on $E_m$. Each smooth $V_\varepsilon$ has identical classical restrictions on the two sides of $F$; by [F2] and the $W^{1,2}$ convergence, their cell traces converge to those of $V$, proving equality of the traces of $\zeta$ on $E_m$. Hence the traces agree in $L^2(F)$. Therefore step 2.1 gives $\|p_K-p_L\|_F\le C h_K^{s+1/2}(A_K+A_L)$. For completeness, the facet evaluation bound holds also for one-dimensional facets when $d=2$: on the fixed reference facet the barycentric affine basis has a positive-definite $L^2$ Gram matrix, because the square integral of every nonzero affine polynomial is positive. Its inverse bounds every vertex coefficient by a constant times the $L^2$ norm; the facet surface Jacobian from [F3] gives exactly $|p(z)|\le C|F|^{-1/2}\|p\|_F$ in every $d\ge2$. This inverse evaluation bound [F4] yields $|p_K(z)-p_L(z)|\le C h_K^{1+s-d/2}(A_K+A_L)$. On a boundary facet containing $z$, [F6] gives zero trace of $\zeta$, so step 2.1 and [F4] give $|p_L(z)|\le C h_L^{1+s-d/2}A_L$. Telescope these bounds along the paths from step 1.2; the interior coefficient is an average over the connected star, and for a boundary vertex use the exposed facet in the component containing $K$. With $\omega_K$ the union of vertex stars of $K$, the bounded valence and local size comparability give $|c_z-p_K(z)|\le C h_K^{1+s-d/2}\left(\sum_{L\in\omega_K}A_L^2\right)^{1/2}.$ [F2, F3, F4, F6, F8, F9, F10, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]

4.1 On $K$, the barycentric basis functions satisfy $\|
abla\phi_z\|_K\le C h_K^{d/2-1}$ by [F3]. Combining step 3.1 with the local volume estimate in step 1.1 gives $\|
abla(\zeta-I_{h,0}\zeta)\|_K\le C h_K^s\left(\sum_{L\in\omega_K}A_L^2ight)^{1/2}.$ The interpolant has zero polynomial trace on every boundary facet because all its boundary-vertex coefficients vanish; the same is true of $\zeta$ by [F6]. Thus the boundary-value term in the comparison seminorm is exactly zero. Since $
abla I_{h,0}\zeta$ is constant on each cell, the intrinsic $s$-seminorm of $
abla(\zeta-I_{h,0}\zeta)$ equals $A_K$ for $s<1$, and its weak derivative is the Hessian of $\zeta$ for $s=1$. Applying [F2] to this gradient and using $h_F\asymp h_K$ from [F3] gives for each boundary facet $F\subset\partial K$ $h_F\|\partial_n(\zeta-I_{h,0}\zeta)\|_F^2\le C h_K^{2s}\sum_{L\in\omega_K}A_L^2.$ [F2, F3, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Each $\omega_K$ has at most $(d+1)N$ cells and each cell occurs in at most $(d+1)N$ such patches. Summing the squared bounds from step 4.1 therefore gives $\|\zeta-I_{h,0}\zeta\|_{\#,h}^2\le C h^{2s}\sum_KA_K^2$. If $s<1$, choose a whole-space extension $Z$ of $\zeta$ within $\varepsilon$ of the restriction norm. Nonnegativity of the pair integrand and disjoint cell interiors imply $\sum_K|\nabla\zeta|_{s,K}^2\le|\nabla Z|_{s,\mathbb R^d}^2\le C\|Z\|_{H^{1+s}(\mathbb R^d)}^2$ by [F1] and [F2]; let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. At $s=1$, the sum of cell Hessian norms is bounded by the global $H^2$ norm of any extension in the same way, then take the infimum. Thus $\sum_KA_K^2\le C\|\zeta\|_{H^{1+s}(\Omega)}^2$. Finally, [F5] puts the continuous zero-boundary affine interpolant in $Y_h$, and the definition of $C_D$ proves the Statement. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F7, A1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume Countable Choice for the cited Sobolev/L2 interface.

Let $K=\{(x,y):x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ x+y\le1\}$, let $f=\mathbf1_{\{x+y\le1/2\}}$, and mark this single cell with $\theta_O=1$. Use the uniform three-generation refinement, any estimator marking fraction, and a per-call budget sufficient for completion.

1.1 The triangle has area $1/2$, while the subtriangle where $f=1$ has area $1/8$, so $\Pi_K^0f=1/4$. Therefore $\|f-\Pi_K^0f\|_2^2=(1/2)(1/4)(3/4)=3/32$. Since $\operatorname{diam}K=\sqrt2$, the initial oscillation square is $3/16$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The region $x+y\le1/2$ is the corner triangle whose other two vertices are the midpoints of the coordinate-axis edges. By [F2] its boundary is a union of refined edges; each refined leaf lies wholly in this region or its complement. Thus $f$ is constant on every child, every child P0 projection is exact, and the refined oscillation is zero. This verifies the strict reduction and agrees with [F3], which gives $\gamma_O=1/4$ at $\theta_O=1$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev and residual-estimator suppliers.

Assume $b=0$, $f$ is constant on each initial cell, and $\mathcal T$ is a conforming descendant. Let $e_\mathcal T$ and $\eta_\mathcal T$ be the exact P1 Galerkin energy error and residual estimator. Let $\mathcal T_*$ be another conforming NVB descendant of $\mathcal T_0$ with exact Galerkin solution $U_*$. ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice, as in the residual and inverse-estimate suppliers.

Suppose the refinement call completes with a matching descendant $\mathcal T_*\ge\mathcal T$ and every cell in the Dörfler estimator set $M_E$ receives three generations of refinement, with exact Galerkin solutions $U,U_*$. For every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\eta_{\mathcal T_*}(U_*)^2\le(1+\varepsilon)\eta_\mathcal T(U)^2-\frac12\eta_\mathcal T(U,M_E)^2+ C_\varepsilon(1+|b|^2h_{\max}^2)\|\nabla(U_*-U)\|_2^2.$$
The constant depends only on $\varepsilon$ and the uniform shape bound.

1.1 Write $d=U_*-U$. On a fine child $K'\subset K$, $R_{K'}(U_*)=R_K(U)-b\cdot
abla d$. Young's inequality gives $h_{K'}^2\|R_{K'}(U_*)\|_2^2\le(1+\varepsilon)h_{K'}^2\|R_K(U)\|_2^2+(1+\varepsilon^{-1})|b|^2h_{K'}^2\|
abla d\|_{L^2(K')}^2.$ Unmarked cells retain the same old volume weight. On marked parents, [F2] makes the old residual part at most one quarter its old value. Summing, and charging closure-refined cells to their old parent, bounds the volume contribution by $(1+\varepsilon)$ times the old volume sum minus $ rac34$ of its marked volume sum, plus $C_\varepsilon |b|^2h_{\max}^2\|
abla d\|_2^2$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 On every split old edge, each subedge length is at most half the parent length and the sum of their lengths is the parent length; hence the sum of squared subedge lengths is at most one half the squared parent length. The old jump is constant along each parent edge, so its inherited contribution is reduced by at least one half whenever its marked cell is refined. On new interior edges within one old parent the old affine gradient has zero jump. The new jump is the old jump plus the jump of $\nabla d$; Young's inequality and [F3] give a remainder at most $C_\varepsilon\|\nabla d\|_2^2$. Assign each old edge half to each incident cell as in the definition. Combining this with step 1.1, the marked cell and edge reductions are at least one half of $\eta_\mathcal T(U,M_E)^2$; absorb the remaining nonnegative reduction into the left inequality to obtain the displayed bound. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

cases.evidence: Identical Galerkin solutions give zero correction term, leaving only reduction of inherited residual weights.
cases.review_reason: Identical Galerkin solutions give zero correction term, leaving only reduction of inherited residual weights.

## Statement

For fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and periodic grid, the smooth-branch weights $w_j^{\varepsilon,h}$ of [[def-periodic-pic-shape-assignment-and-gather]] are $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb T_L^d$. For every multi-index $\beta$, $\max_j\|\partial^\beta w_j^{\varepsilon,h}\|_\infty<\infty$. They are nonnegative and sum to one at every point.

1.1 By [F2], each numerator in [F1] is a smooth periodic function. The finite sum defining $Z_{\varepsilon,h}$ is smooth and strictly positive; compactness gives a positive minimum. The reciprocal of a positive smooth function is smooth, so every ratio $w_j^{\varepsilon,h}$ is $C^\infty$. Each derivative is continuous on the compact torus and hence bounded; there are finitely many indices $j$, so their maximum is finite. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Each weight is nonnegative by [F1] and positivity of $\eta_\varepsilon$. Summing [F1] over $j$ gives $\sum_jw_j^{\varepsilon,h}(x)=Z_{\varepsilon,h}(x)/Z_{\varepsilon,h}(x)=1$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Write $q=k\cos\theta$ for $0\le\theta<\pi/2$. The reflected amplitude is
$$\mathcal R(\theta)=\frac{\cos\theta-1}{\cos\theta+1}.$$
It is $0$ at normal incidence, equals $-1/3$ at $\theta=\pi/3$, and tends to $-1$ at grazing incidence.

1.1 Divide numerator and denominator of [F1] by $k>0$ to obtain $\mathcal R=(\cos\theta-1)/(\cos\theta+1)$. At $\theta=0$, this is $0$; at $\theta=\pi/3$, $\cos\theta=1/2$ and it is $(-1/2)/(3/2)=-1/3$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 As $\theta\uparrow\pi/2$, continuity of cosine gives $\cos\theta\to0$ and the denominator tends to $1$, so $\mathcal R\to-1$ and $|\mathcal R|\to1$. The endpoint is a limit; the propagating theorem assumed $q>0$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Write $q=k\cos\theta$ for $0\le\theta<\pi/2$. The reflected amplitude is
$$\mathcal R(\theta)=\frac{\cos\theta-1}{\cos\theta+1}.$$
It is $0$ at normal incidence, equals $-1/3$ at $\theta=\pi/3$, and tends to $-1$ at grazing incidence.

1.1 Divide numerator and denominator of [F1] by $k>0$ to obtain $\mathcal R=(\cos\theta-1)/(\cos\theta+1)$. At $\theta=0$, this is $0$; at $\theta=\pi/3$, $\cos\theta=1/2$ and it is $(-1/2)/(3/2)=-1/3$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 As $\theta\uparrow\pi/2$, continuity of cosine gives $\cos\theta\to0$ and the denominator tends to $1$, so $\mathcal R\to-1$ and $|\mathcal R|\to1$. The endpoint is a limit; the propagating theorem assumed $q>0$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the model, positive Schur operators, and algorithm of [[def-ale-linear-diffusion-transmission-model]], [[lem-ale-schur-complement-positive-and-minimizes-energy]], and [[alg-ale-robin-robin-partitioned-iteration]], with $\alpha>0$. Every Robin solve in the algorithm exists uniquely, and for every admitted input it returns `converged` with the current first-subdomain trace on the first passing test, or returns `budget_exhausted` with $\lambda_1^M$ after at most $M$ passes. Let $\lambda_*$ be the unique monolithic trace solving $(S_1+S_2)\lambda_*=f_1+f_2$, and put $R_i=(\alpha I-S_i)(\alpha I+S_i)^{-1}$ and $q_i=\|R_i\|$, $q=q_1q_2$. Then $q<1$, the unique fixed point of the iteration corresponds exactly to $\lambda_*$, and the incoming-data error satisfies

$$r_1^{m+1}-r_1^*=R_2R_1(r_1^m-r_1^*),\qquad\|r_1^{m+1}-r_1^*\|\le q\|r_1^m-r_1^*\|.$$

If the algorithm's stop test succeeds at pass $m+1$, its returned trace satisfies $\|\lambda_1^{m+1}-\lambda_*\|\le\varepsilon$. A `budget_exhausted` return carries no such certificate.

1.1 For each $i$, $S_i+\alpha I$ is self-adjoint positive definite because $\langle(S_i+\alpha I)z,z\rangle=\langle S_i z,z\rangle+\alpha\|z\|^2>0$ for every $z\ne0$. It is therefore invertible on the finite-dimensional space $\Lambda$; its inverse and the operators $R_i$ have finite norms, and $\|(\alpha I+S_1)^{-1}\|>0$ because $\Lambda\ne\{0\}$. Each first solve uniquely determines $\lambda_1^{m+1}$, the first exchange uniquely determines $r_2^{m+1}$, the second solve uniquely determines $\lambda_2^{m+1}$, and the last exchange uniquely determines $r_1^{m+1}$. Since $M$ is finite, these operations define all passes up to $M$; the tests either return `converged` at the first pass that satisfies them or, if none does, return `budget_exhausted` with the last trace. Thus the algorithm is well-defined and terminates within its stated budget. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 By [F1] and [F2], $S:=S_1+S_2$ is positive definite, so the monolithic trace $\lambda_*=S^{-1}(f_1+f_2)$ exists uniquely. Set $p_i^*:=S_i\lambda_*-f_i$; then $p_1^*+p_2^*=0$. Define $r_1^*:=\alpha\lambda_*+p_1^*$ and $r_2^*:=\alpha\lambda_*+p_2^*$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The first Robin equation in [F3] is equivalent to $r_1=\alpha\lambda_1+p_1$, and its exchange is $r_2=\alpha\lambda_1-p_1$; the second equation and exchange have the same forms with indices 1 and 2 reversed. Since $p_2^*=-p_1^*$, the pair $(r_1^*,r_2^*)$ is unchanged by both exchanges, so $\lambda_*$ gives a fixed point. [F1, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Conversely, at any fixed point the two exchange equalities give $r_2=\alpha\lambda_1-p_1=\alpha\lambda_2+p_2$ and $r_1=\alpha\lambda_1+p_1=\alpha\lambda_2-p_2$. Adding the equalities for $r_2$ and $r_1$ yields $2\alpha(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)=0$, hence $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$; subtracting yields $p_1+p_2=0$. Thus the common trace solves the unique monolithic equation from step 1.2, proving the fixed point is unique. [F1, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By [F2] and [F4], in an orthonormal eigenbasis of $S_i$, $R_i$ has eigenvalues $(\alpha-\sigma)/(\alpha+\sigma)$ with $\sigma>0$. Each has absolute value strictly below $1$, so $q_i<1$. Subtracting the fixed-point equations from the iteration equations in [F3] gives $r_2^{m+1}-r_2^*=R_1(r_1^m-r_1^*)$ and then $r_1^{m+1}-r_1^*=R_2(r_2^{m+1}-r_2^*)$. Therefore the displayed error map holds and $q=q_1q_2<1$. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Put $e_m=r_1^m-r_1^*$ and $d_m=r_1^{m+1}-r_1^m$. The error map in step 3.1 gives $d_m=(R_2R_1-I)e_m$. Since $\|R_2R_1\|\le q<1$, the reverse triangle inequality yields $\|d_m\|\ge(1-q)\|e_m\|$. The first solve in [F3] gives $\lambda_1^{m+1}-\lambda_*=(\alpha I+S_1)^{-1}e_m$. Therefore the stop test in [F3] implies $\|\lambda_1^{m+1}-\lambda_*\|\le\|(\alpha I+S_1)^{-1}\|\,\|d_m\|/(1-q)\le\varepsilon$. If the finite pass budget is exhausted without this test, no trace certificate has been issued. [F3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Choose integers $N_j\ge3$, a number $M\ge1$ of time steps, and
$\tau=T/M$. Sample $u_0$ at the grid nodes of
[[def-na-periodic-grid-and-tensor-multilinear-interpolation]] and set
$U_i^0=u_0(x_i)$. At each $n=0,\ldots,M-1$, compute
$$U_i^{n+1}=\min_{a\in A_k}\left\{ I_hU^n\bigl(x_i+\tau b_a(x_i,t_n)\bigr)+\tau\ell_a(x_i,t_n) \right\},\qquad t_n=n\tau.$$
The position is evaluated on the torus, so its coordinates wrap modulo one.
The algorithm always uses a finite nonempty set $A_k\subset A$. For a finite
control model take $A_k=A$; for a compact control model, supply finite sets
whose Hamiltonian errors $\eta_k(R)$ from
[[def-na-first-order-hjb-cauchy-problem]] tend to zero on every bounded
momentum set. This is the declared finite-control approximation branch; it
does not presume an unimplemented continuous minimization oracle. Return
$U^M$.

The update is the explicit Euler-footpoint semi-Lagrangian branch specified by
the plan. It defines its footpoint and interpolant locally; no unauthored
characteristic-flow estimate is presumed.

## Statement

Assume full AC conservatively for the declared weighted-$L^2$ Hilbert dependency. Let $\Omega$ be an admitted domain with its uniform cone constants, fix $d\ge1$, $\nu>0$, $s=\nu+d/2$, and choose an integer $m>\nu$. There exist $C,h_0>0$, depending only on $d,s,m$ and the cone constants, such that for every finite nonempty $X\subset\Omega$ of fill distance $h=h_X\le h_0$ and every $u\in H^s(\Omega)$ with $u|_X=0$,
$$\|u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le C h^\nu\|u\|_{H^s(\Omega)}.$$
The estimate has no separation or mesh-ratio hypothesis.

1.1 Since $\Omega$ is a nonempty open domain, it contains a ball $B(z,r)$. For $d\ge1$ this ball contains the infinitely many distinct points $z+ rac{r}{2n}e_1$, $n\ge1$, by [F6]. The finite set $X$ omits one such point $x$, so $\min_{y\in X}|x-y|>0$ and therefore $h_X\ge\min_{y\in X}|x-y|>0$. In particular $h^{-1}$ is defined. Fix any whole-space extension $U=U_g$ of $u$, and split $g=g_{m lo}+g_{m hi}$ with $g_{m lo}=g\mathbf1_{\{|\xi|\le h^{-1}\}}$. Let $V=U_{g_{m lo}}$ and $W=U_{g_{m hi}}$. By Cauchy--Schwarz [F5], polar integration [F3], and $s=
u+d/2$, $$\|W\|_\infty\le\left(\int_{|\xi|>h^{-1}}(1+|\xi|^2)^{-s}d\xiight)^{1/2}\|U\|_{H^s}\le C h^
u\|U\|_{H^s}.$$ Indeed, for $r\ge h^{-1}\ge1$ the radial tail is at most $C\int_{h^{-1}}^\infty r^{-2
u-1}dr=C'h^{2
u}$. [F1, F3, F5, F6, A1, algebra]

2.1 For each multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|=m$, the bounded frequency support makes $D^\alpha V$ well defined and continuous by differentiation under an absolutely integrable Fourier integral. Cauchy--Schwarz [F5] and polar coordinates give $$\|D^\alpha V\|_\infty\le C\left(\int_{|\xi|\le h^{-1}}|\xi|^{2m}(1+|\xi|^2)^{-s}d\xiight)^{1/2}\|U\|_{H^s}\le C h^{
u-m}\|U\|_{H^s}.$$ For the last estimate, the radial integral on $r\le1$ is finite and on $1\le r\le h^{-1}$ is bounded by $C\int_1^{h^{-1}}r^{2m-2
u-1}dr\le C'h^{-2(m-
u)}$, using $m>
u$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $x\in\Omega$ and choose the stencil from [F2]. Taylor-expand the globally defined smooth $V$ at $x$ to degree $m-1$. The segment from $x$ to each $y_j$ lies in $\mathbb R^d$, where $V$ is smooth, so [F3] bounds each remainder by $C|y_j-x|^m\max_{|\alpha|=m}\|D^\alpha V\|_\infty$. The polynomial part cancels under the stencil's reproduction identities. ## Statement

Assume a real, mean-zero, weakly stationary process $X_t$ satisfies the causal AR(1) model
$$X_t=\tfrac12X_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$$
in $L^2$, where $\varepsilon_t$ is centered with variance $3/4$, is uncorrelated with $X_s$ for every $s<t$, and the process is weakly stationary. Here “AR(1)” means precisely this first-order autoregression; the stated uncorrelatedness is the innovation orthogonality used below. Then its autocovariance function (ACVF) is $\gamma(h)=2^{-|h|}$. The order-two Durbin–Levinson output is $\phi_2=(1/2,0)^T$ and $\nu_2=3/4$. Separately, for $T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $b=(1,1)^T$, the general-RHS Hermitian Toeplitz solver returns $T^{-1}b=(2/3,2/3)^T$ by the Gohberg–Semencul formula.

1.1 Centering and weak stationarity give $E[X_t]=0$ and $\gamma(0)=\operatorname{Var}(X_t)$ for every $t$. From the autoregression and innovation orthogonality, $$\gamma(0)=\operatorname{Var}(\tfrac12X_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t)=\tfrac14\gamma(0)+\tfrac34,$$ so $\gamma(0)=1$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For the separate general-RHS solve, set $T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1\end{pmatrix}$ as in the Statement. For each nonzero $z\in\mathbb C^2$, $z^*Tz=|z_1+z_2/2|^2+3|z_2|^2/4>0$, so $T$ is Hermitian positive definite. Its first lag data are $t_0=1,t_1=1/2$, hence $\alpha_1=t_1/t_0=1/2$, $\phi_1=\alpha_1=1/2$, and $\nu_1=t_0(1-|\alpha_1|^2)=3/4$. The endpoint columns from [F5] are $$v=(-2/3,4/3)^T,\qquad u=J_2v=(4/3,-2/3)^T,\qquad u_0=4/3>0.$$ The lower triangular Toeplitz products are $$L(u)L(u)^*=\begin{pmatrix}16/9&-8/9\\-8/9&20/9\end{pmatrix},\qquad L(Z_2v)L(Z_2v)^*=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&4/9\end{pmatrix}.$$ Therefore the formula in [F5] gives $$T^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}4/3&-2/3\\-2/3&4/3\end{pmatrix},\qquad T^{-1}b=(2/3,2/3)^T.$$ Direct multiplication also verifies $T(2/3,2/3)^T=(1,1)^T$. [given, F5, algebra]

2.1 For each integer $h\ge1$, covariance bilinearity and $\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_t,X_{t-h})=0$ give $$\gamma(h)=\operatorname{Cov}(X_t,X_{t-h})=\tfrac12\gamma(h-1).$$ Induction yields $\gamma(h)=2^{-h}$ for $h\ge0$; covariance symmetry gives $\gamma(-h)=\gamma(h)$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, induction]

3.1 The order-one recursion gives $\kappa_1=\gamma(1)/\gamma(0)=1/2$, $\phi_1=(1/2)$ and $
u_1=1(1-1/4)=3/4$. At order two, $$\kappa_2= rac{\gamma(2)-\phi_{1,1}\gamma(1)}{
u_1}= rac{1/4-(1/2)(1/2)}{3/4}=0,$$ so $\phi_2=(\phi_{1,1}-\kappa_2\phi_{1,1},\kappa_2)^T=(1/2,0)^T$ and $
u_2=
u_1(1-\kappa_2^2)=3/4$. By steps 1.1 and 2.1, $\Gamma_1=[1]$ and $\Gamma_2=T$. Step 1.2 proves $T$ Hermitian positive definite, so the real leading covariance blocks are positive definite; [F3] applies and [F4] identifies this vector as the unique prediction solution. [given, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The first calculation reuses the published real covariance prediction recursion, while the second is a distinct arbitrary-right-hand-side Hermitian Toeplitz solve; the computed vector satisfies its stated system. [step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Take the unit cubic torus $\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$, with charges $q_1=1$ at
$x_1=(0,0,0)$ and $q_2=-1$ at $x_2=(1/2,0,0)$. The dipole is neutral and its
Fourier structure factor vanishes on every even first-coordinate mode and is
equal to $2$ on every odd first-coordinate mode.

1.1 The two positions are distinct in $\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$ and $q_1+q_2=0$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^3$, [F1] gives $\rho_k=1-e^{-2\pi i k_1/2}=1-(-1)^{k_1}$; hence $\rho_0=0$, $\rho_k=0$ when $k_1$ is even, and $\rho_k=2$ when $k_1$ is odd. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For any finite symmetric reciprocal mode set $\mathcal K$, the dipole contributes $\frac12\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}c_k|\rho_k|^2=2\sum_{k\in\mathcal K,\,k_1\text{ odd}}c_k$ to the retained reciprocal energy. The remaining real-space and self contributions are exactly the terms in [F2], under its neutrality and Countable Choice hypotheses [A1]. Thus the zero mode is absent and the reciprocal selection is precisely the odd-$k_1$ subset, not an assumed continuum average. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Take scalar CARE data $A=B=C=R=1$ and the stabilizing starting gain $K_0=2$.

1.1 At $K_0=2$, the closed loop is $-1$ and the exact Lyapunov equation gives $-2X_0+5=0$, hence $X_0=5/2$ and $K_1=5/2$. The next closed loop is $-3/2$, and its policy equation gives $-3X_1+1+25/4=0$, hence $X_1=29/12<5/2$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Consider instead an unchecked approximate policy value $\widetilde P=0$, which proposes $\widetilde K=0$. A full step gives closed loop $A-B\widetilde K=1$, which is unstable. More generally, a line-search trial between $K_0=2$ and $0$ has $K\in[0,2]$. If $K\le1$ its closed loop $1-K$ is not Hurwitz. If $1<K<2$, its exact cost matrix is $P(K)=(1+K^2)/(2(K-1))$, and $P(K)-\frac52=\frac{(K-2)(K-3)}{2(K-1)}>0.$ Thus every nonzero trial either loses stability or increases cost; the certified safeguard rejects it. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For $n\ge1$ and $\alpha,\beta>-1$, the measure and order-$2n-1$ moment datum in [[def-gauss-jacobi-quadrature-rule]] are valid Gaussian quadrature data. In particular the monic orthogonal polynomial exists, its $n$ roots are distinct points of $(-1,1)$, and the Lagrange weights and finite rule are well-defined.

1.1 By [F1], the measure is finite and positive, all required moments are finite, and each of the $n+1$ explicit points $t_j=-1+2j/n$ for $j=0,\ldots,n$ lies in its support; these points are distinct because $n\ge1$. Thus the data satisfy [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra, construct]

2.1 Applying [F4] to the moment datum of step 1.1 gives distinct roots in $(-1,1)$, nonzero node differences, finite Lagrange-weight integrals, and a finite rule. These are exactly the asserted well-definedness properties in [F3]. [F3, F4, step 1.1] ∎

## Example

For $f_B(s)=s^2/2$, use the Godunov flux $G$ of
[[def-godunov-flux-for-burgers]] on cells of width $h_m\downarrow0$ with
$\tau_m=h_m/2$. Let $u_0(x)=1$ for $x<0$ and $u_0(x)=-1$ for $x>0$, with
cell-average initialization. The scheme preserves the stationary shock exactly:
$$ U_j^{m,n}=\begin{cases}1,&j<0,\\-1,&j\ge0.\end{cases} $$
Its reconstruction is the same stationary weak shock for every $m$. The
Rankine–Hugoniot speed is $0$, which is the speed of this limit.
1.1 The cell averages are $1$ for $j<0$ and $-1$ for $j\ge0$. The only face pairs are $(1,1)$, $(1,-1)$, and $(-1,-1)$; [F3] gives flux $1/2$ in all three cases. [F1, F3, given]

2.1 Every cell therefore has equal left and right fluxes at every step, so the update leaves every $U_j^{m,n}$ unchanged. Induction on $n$ gives exactly the stationary step profile displayed in the Example. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The reconstruction equals that stationary profile almost everywhere for all $m$, so it converges strongly in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and is bounded by $1$. The weak-limit theorem [F4] applies. [F2, F4, step 2.1, given]
4.1 The traces are $u^-=1$ and $u^+=-1$. Thus [F5] gives $s=(f_B(-1)-f_B(1))/(-1-1)=(1/2-1/2)/(-2)=0$, agreeing with the stationary interface. [F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $K$ be a convex set in the state domain, and consider a periodic uniform
mesh and one first-order HLL update as defined in
[[def-pe03-first-order-hll-finite-volume-update]]. Assume every cell mean
$U_i\in K$. At every face impose the **HLL fan-average hypothesis** that the
two adjacent half-cell averages $A^-,A^+$ from
[[lem-pe03-hll-half-cell-riemann-averages]] lie in $K$, with that lemma's local
CFL bounds. Then every updated mean $U_i^+$ belongs to $K$. A sufficient
condition for the fan-average hypothesis is that every HLL intermediate state
$U_*\in K$, because the stated CFL makes each half-cell average a convex
combination of a cell state and $U_*$. The result does not assert a bound on
exact nonlinear wave speeds.

1.1 At each face, the stated HLL fan-average hypothesis gives $A^-,A^+\in K$. In the sufficient intermediate-state case, the CFL bounds make the coefficients in each formula of [F2] nonnegative and sum to one, so convexity and $U_L,U_R,U_*\in K$ give the same conclusion. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], $U_i^+=\tfrac12(A^+_{i-1/2}+A^-_{i+1/2})$. This is a convex combination of two members of $K$, so $U_i^+\in K$ for every cell. The argument is one-step and uses only the supplied HLL speeds and the explicit CFL bounds. [given, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F(\widehat x)=A\widehat x+b$ be an orientation-preserving affine bijection between nondegenerate $d$-simplices, with $J=\det A>0$, and use the contravariant Piola map of [[def-na-contravariant-piola-map]]. For every $k\ge0$, it maps $\operatorname{RT}_k(\widehat K)$ bijectively onto $\operatorname{RT}_k(K)$, and for every $k\ge1$ it maps $\operatorname{BDM}_k(\widehat K)$ bijectively onto $\operatorname{BDM}_k(K)$.

1.1 For BDM, if $\widehat v\in\mathbb P_k(\widehat K)^d$, then $\widehat v\circ F^{-1}$ is a vector polynomial of degree at most $k$ in $x$ because $F^{-1}$ is affine. Multiplication by the constant matrix $J^{-1}A$ preserves this degree, so [F1] maps BDM into BDM. Applying the same argument to the inverse affine map proves onto-ness. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Write an RT field as $\widehat v(\widehat x)=\widehat p(\widehat x)+\widehat x\widehat q(\widehat x)$ with $\widehat p\in\mathbb P_k^d$ and homogeneous $\widehat q$ of degree $k$. The push-forward of the first term is in $\mathbb P_k^d$. For the second term, use $\widehat x=A^{-1}(x-b)$: its image is $J^{-1}(x-b)\widehat q(A^{-1}(x-b))$. The scalar polynomial $\widehat q(A^{-1}(x-b))$ has highest homogeneous part $q_k(x):=\widehat q(A^{-1}x)$ of degree $k$, with remainder of degree at most $k-1$. Thus $(x-b)\widehat q(A^{-1}(x-b))=xq_k(x)+p_k(x)$ for some vector polynomial $p_k$ of degree at most $k$: all terms from $x$ times the remainder and from $b$ times the full scalar polynomial have degree at most $k$. Therefore the image lies in $\operatorname{RT}_k(K)$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The inverse Piola map is the contravariant Piola map for the orientation-preserving affine bijection $F^{-1}$, up to the displayed inverse formula in [F1]. The same polynomial decomposition from step 1.2 applied to $F^{-1}$ maps $\operatorname{RT}_k(K)$ into $\operatorname{RT}_k(\widehat K)$. Hence the forward inclusion is onto. [F1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the mesh conventions of [[def-na-simplicial-mesh-rt-bdm-spaces]]. With $V_h=\operatorname{RT}_0(\mathcal T_h)\cap H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$, $Q_h=\mathbb P_0(\mathcal T_h)\cap L^2_0(D)$ and $b(v_h,q_h)=-\int_Dq_h\operatorname{div}v_h$, the discrete kernel
$$Z_h:=\{v_h\in V_h:b(v_h,q_h)=0\text{ for every }q_h\in Q_h\}$$
is exactly $\{v_h\in V_h:\operatorname{div}v_h=0\}$.
1.1 By [F2], $\operatorname{div}v_h$ is cellwise constant; by [F1], its global mean is zero. Thus $\operatorname{div}v_h\in Q_h$. [A1, given, F1, F2]

2.1 If $v_h\in Z_h$, test its defining orthogonality with the admissible choice $q_h=\operatorname{div}v_h$ from step 1.1. Then $0=b(v_h,q_h)=-\|\operatorname{div}v_h\|_{L^2(D)}^2$, so its divergence vanishes in $L^2$. Conversely, if $\operatorname{div}v_h=0$, the defining integral $b(v_h,q_h)$ is zero for every $q_h\in Q_h$. This proves the equality, including the case $Q_h=\{0\}$. [given, step 1.1, algebra, cases] ∎
